Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 44, to amend the Immigration Act.
Explain.

As the Immigration Act now stands, it is possible for a variety of causes to deport people, no matter how long they have resided in Canada. Last year there were several cases that aroused a good deal of public interest, one case in which a woman was deported after some eighteen years' residence in Canada. Her connections in the old country had been broken up; she had during all those years established connections in this country and suddenly, because of some physical ailment of a rather serious character, she was deported. There have been a large number of cases of a similar character. Therefore I propose in this amendment that there should be no deportation after ten years' continuous residence. Just as in certain insurance policies there is a definite period after which the policy becomes non-contestable, after ten years' continuous residence in this country no one could be deported.
The second clause relates to those who have been resident for ten years in Canada and who may have been forced to go, we will say, to the United States for a short period to seek work. They very often find themselves unable to return to this country although they have lived here for a large number of years, and there have been certain cases where they have been threatened with deportation to the countries from which they originally came. The second clause would permit them, if everything else was all right, to enter Canada on account of their having resided in this country for ten years. I might put it a little more correctly in this way: after ten years' residence in Canada, they would not be precluded from reentering this country simply for the reason that they had gone elsewhere on this continent for a short period.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver South) moved_ for leave to introduce Bill No. 45, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
Canada Shipping Act
Explain.

The present Canada
Shipping Act is a rather old piece of legislation, and very much out of harmony with modern industrial conditions. The purpose of these amendments is to put the conditions under which seamen have to live and work more in line with modern industrial standards.
The first amendment provides for the physical examination of seamen. There is no provision for that in the present act. It has been brought to my attention that on occasions seamen suffering from contagious or infectious diseases have been taken aboard ship, or they have been taken ill after coming on board, thus creating a menace to the health of the other members of the crew.
The next amendment provides for more efficient inspection of water and provisions supplied for the crew than now prevails. At the present time the act provides only that the seamen may complain and if their complaint is not upheld by the person making the inspection, they are penalized for making the complaint. It also provides for a scale of provisions for the crew, somewhat more extensive than that for which the regulations now provides. There is also a provision for regulation of the hours of work and for compensation to seamen injured in the course of their employment. There is another provision that only ships registered in Canada shall engage in the coastal trade of Canada.

* DUTY ON POTATOES
speechtext:
1.	In view of the fact that Cuba has intimated her intention of increasing the duty

against Canada on potatoes and other products, has the government taken any action to arrange some trade agreement to prevent this increase?
2.	If so, have they been successful, and what is the nature of the agreement?

subtopic: * DUTY ON POTATOES
speechtext:
1.	Yes, the government sent a representative to Havana for the purpose of conferring with the Cuban government regarding better trade arrangements between the two countries.
2.	No agreement has yet been arrived at. Under present economic conditions there, especially in view of the depressed condition of the market for their principal product, sugar, lately selling at $1150 per cwt. while the production cost is about $2, the policy of the Cuban government is to encourage more diversified agricultural production by means of tariff protection on potatoes and other items. They are, however, willing to further discuss these matters, and this government is now giving consideration to proposals in that regard.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, for every one hundred dollars spent on war one dollar should be spent to promote peace by instituting international professorships and scholarships in leading Canadian universities.
She said: I spoke on a similar matter last year, there was then quite a long debate on it, and I hope therefore that we shall not now find it necessary to consume ifiuch of the time of the house. The resolution last year was referred to the committee on industrial and international relations and that committee called four witnessess as follows:
Dr. O. D. Skelton, Under Secretary of State, Department of External Affairs.
Mr. Graham Spry, national secretary of the associated Canadian Clubs.
Dr. Norman A. Mackenzie, L.L.M., head of the Department of International Law, of Toronto university.
Professor P. E. Corbett, dean of the Faculty of Law, McGill university.

Dr. H. M. Tory, president of the League of Nations Society of Canada submitted a written memorandum. Letters from Dr. Murray, president of the university of Saskatchewan, Professor R. A. MacKay, of Dal-housie university, and Dr. Robert C. Wallace, of the university of Alberta, were also submitted to the chairman and were embodied in the report.
The committee reported back to the house and since the report is very brief, I want to give it to the house. They said:
1.	That the facilities that now exist in the Department of External Affairs should be extended and increased, especially in regard to the spreading of information on the international relations of Canada with other countries in the commonwealth of British nations, and also with other nations of the world. Your committee are of the opinion that this department is doing excellent work along these lines and recommend for your consideration the establishment of a central research library on inter-imperial and international matters in connection with the department.
2.	That the whole subject be given further consideration by a committee of the house at the next session of parliament.
It is because of the last paragraph in the report of the committee that I am again addressing the house on the subject. While the witnesses before the committee did not all agree with each other, nor did the members of the committee all think we ought to have chairs on international relations in the universities, nor did they all think we should have scholarships on international affairs in the universities, still there was a feeling in the committee and I think it was unanimous that Canada does lack in those facilities which will fit our young men and women, graduating from the universities, to become servants of Canada in our legations abroad or to serve Canada well in the field of research or journalism or the many other things requiring extensive knowledge of international affairs. As a matter of fact, I think we can go so far as to say that some understanding of international affairs and of the relation of Canada to the world as a whole, is required bv everyone twenty-one years of age and over. Everyone who votes today ought to have at least some understanding-and the greater the understanding the better-of international affairs.
Because I know what a lot of evidence and reports come to the desks of members. I am aware how difficult it is to find time to read them, so I want to review as briefly as I can some of the points made by the witnesses. Mr. Norman Mackenzie, who, as I said a moment ago, is head of the department of International Law in the university of Tor-

International Peace-Miss Macphail
onto, stressed the fact that we have not the library facilities that we should have. He said:
I know myself that our libraries are not adequate and any method of assistance that the government ean suggest would be desirable, and 1 am sure would be accepted.
At another place he says:
You might establish in Ottawa a library on international law and international relations in connection with the Department of External Affairs, in connection with the library of parliament, or in connection with the Archives. That is one way. Students would come here in their spare time, vacations and so on, to study.
Then, he gave another suggestion which seemed to me to have merit. He said:
I suggest that the Department pf External Affairs, in addition to the publications that it does issue from time to time, should compile each year a volume of those documents that are not seoret, those documents that are public documents, relating to international or interimperial affairs in Canada, and include with them the debates in Hansard on international affairs and imperial affairs. I think that kind of publication would be of great value to students of international law and international relations, not only in Canada but all over the world.
Dean. Corbett also made it clear that he did not believe that we had the facilities in our universities that we ought to have. Dr. Murphy asked Dean Corbett this question:
Do you feel our Canadian universities have not been keeping apace, in growth and knowledge, on international subjects?
Dean Corbett replied:
I am afraid that that is true. I think that the universities have lagged behind, that they have not recognized the charms and the importance of international affairs as a medium of liberal education, for one thing. I think that may be explained by the lack of money, but not' entirely. There has been a tendency among the universities to regard university training as to being exclusively aimed at the preparation of men for a business or professional life in this country, and too little attention to fitting them for life as members of the human community.
Professor R. A. MacKay of Dalhousie university told something of his work. He said that he taught the subjects of international law and international relations at Princeton and Cornell universities, and also at Dalhousie, and returned to Canada three years ago. He said:
Since my return to Canada three years ago, I have been more and. more impressed with our deficiencies in teaching international relations in Canada. In the first place, there is relatively little attention given to the field in our universities. Secondly, the facilities for teaching the subject in Canada are utterly inadequate. Rot a single library is adequately equipped for research work, except in isolated
subjects. In this respect eastern Canada is, perhaps, the worst section of Canada. For example, so far as I am aware, there is no collection of the British Accounts and Papers, or British, Foreign and State Papers, or British Hansard, in the maritime provinces. Nor is there any complete collection of the League of Nations papers, nor American government documents.
The same professor also said:
We need to train experts for public service, for teaching, for research, for journalism and other activities. At present there are really no adequate facilities for this in this country.
Dr. Skelton gave a most excellent speech. I shall not go into it because he did not give those short quotations that suit my purpose at the moment; but his speech is well worth reading by every member who has not already done so. Dr. Skelton, while he was very careful, admitted that much more could be done than was being done to fit students to function well in the realm of international affairs.
I am going to suppose that members of the house will Say: Whale this may be very good, it cannot be done because education is a matter over which the provinces have jurisdiction, and we cannot interfere. I want to quote what was said on that point by Dr. Skelton, Professor Mackenzie and Dean Corbett. May I quote from Dr. Skelton first. Speaking of scholarships he said:
They (the Dominion government) could establish scolarships without incurring the discrimination involved in selecting this institution or that institution for the grant of funds for a chair of international relations.
He goes on:
There is, further, a certain precedent in the aid given by the Dominion government to the National Research Council, which uses a large part of its federal grant, in establishing bursaries and scholarships to students in the natural sciences, though these are practically all used for graduate work in Canada itself.
I want the members to recall that Professor Mackenzie teaches international law, and in speaking of this difficulty of the provinces having jurisdiction over education, he says:
Now, among other things, I teach constitutional law, and realize that there are certain difficulties in the way of the Dominion government, or the federal parliament, interfering with the rights of the provinces.
Further on he said:
But I do feel that there are steps that the Dominion government ean and should take to bring the matter of education in international relations to the attention of the authorities in the provinces. One of the methods that I would suggest to the people that are interested in such things is the method that has been adopted by the Department of National Defence.

1454	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macphail
He goes into that method a little more fully. Dean Corbett, who is also a professor of law, in dealing with this point said that onee the principle was agreed to, he felt that anything that stood in the way of its being carried out could be overcome. Last year the then Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), speaking to my resolution, on March the 6th, said, at page 354 of Hansard:
By a request from the provinces or by negotiations of some kind a way might be found to effect the purpose of the resolution.
So we have all these authorities saying that if the government really wanted to give a grant to the universities of the provinces, a way to do it could be found. I agree with that, because I have noticed in this house that when the government really wants to make a grant, there are ways found to get around any difficulty. The cadet grant which goes to the provinces is certainly one instance, and another is the grants for technical education. Then, too, the federal government has charge of peace and war. It is their business to prepare the country so that if we go into a war we shall win. Those who believe that we can win security best by armaments rely upon the federal government for the armaments. So I think it is perfectly fair to say that if the Dominion government are looked to by the people of Canada to win security through armaments, they should also be looked to to secure security through other methods, one of them being education. We are spending a very great sum of money yet for armaments and military preparation. Possibly over 40 per cent of our total budget goes on war account, past and in preparation. So, while I am not stressing the one dollar for every hundred, because to me that would only be the thin edge of the wedge, I do not feel that it is too much to ask the Dominion government to give some leadership in this matter, and leadership in a financial way, to the universities to help them prepare graduate students to function well in the realm of international affairs.	[DOT]
I want to quote again, because it is really the evidence that I am most concerned with, what these men said might be done. Professor Mackenzie gave the sort of evidence that can easily be quoted from. He said:
I am not particular how it is done, but I do think that it is of great value to have as many young men and young women as we can from our country going to other countries for their post-graduate work. They go to Prance; they go to Germany; they go to Italy; they go to Great Britain; to the United States. They come back with a different attitude toward international relations and toward the opinions and ideas and cultures of other peoples.

And President Wallace, in the letter which he sent to the chairman of the committee, also stressed this point. He said:
My feeling is that scholarships sufficient in attractiveness to give our best men an opportunity to spend some time at Geneva and elsewhere in Europe would on the whole be the best service that could be provided to stimulate interest and knowledge in international affairs. As a rule it is not possible for universities with their relatively limited finances to provide such scholarships and we have to rely on public-minded citizens who are interested in this work or the Dominion of Canada to help out in financing such schemes.
Professor Murray of the university of Saskatchewan referred to the benefit they had received from the fact that certain of their professors had gone abroad. He said:
It seems to me the greatest assistance could be derived from travelling scholarships enabling students and teachers of the university to see conditions at Geneva and Europe at first hand. This opinion is given because of our experience here.
Two students and one professor, Mr. Simpson, Professor of History, were enabled to visit Geneva and study conditions in Europe and they returned ardent advocates of the League of Nations and firmly convinced of the necessity of promoting a better understanding among peoples of the world.
He stated further that it would be worth while for other people to go. As members of the committee will recall, Professor Skelton made a suggestion. His suggestion was that in examinations for the position of first, second and third secretaries of the Department of External Affairs those who stood first in the examinations would be appointed in the usual way to their positions in the department. Those who came next in the list would be given an opportunity at the expense of the Dominion government to go to Europe themselves, to attach to one of the legations for part of the year, and then to spend the rest of the year in a foreign university. The reference is rather long and I am not quoting the exact words. This winter I read with great interest a book entitled "Learning and Leadership" by Alfred Zimmern. I found in it a sentence which fits my resolution very well. In this book Mr. Zimmern discusses the great need of education because of our changed position in this world wherein the interdependence of nations plays so great a part. At page 54 I find the following:
The opening of the mind to international understanding is indeed not a special luxury for the few. It is an indispensable concomitant of democracy. It goes with the vote. "We must educate our masters," said an English statesman at a moment when the suffrage had been widely extended but no system of general popular education yet brought into being.

International Peace-Mr. Guthrie
And then he adds:
We are in a similar perilous interlude to-day. We have established an international political organization without providing the people with the means for understanding or controlling it.
That statement I feel is true, and it is because I feel it is true that again I urge the house to do something to help the universities prepare our people for the new responsibilities upon them. Dr. Skelton in his rather lengthy but most excellent speech before the committee stressed the shrinking character of the world to-day. He pointed out that humanity is one, and that we must know much more about each other than we have in the past. That for which I am asking in this resolution is not new. The national government of France has done a great deal to provide scholarships and to encourage students to come from other countries to their country, and to enable French students to study abroad. There are departments of international relations in several universities. There is one in the national college of Wales, and another at the London School of Economics. I might mention that Professor Zimmern was the first professor of international relations in the college of Wales. Many American universities have such a department and while Cambridge and Oxford do not so designate the departments, they have eight or more professors lecturing on international law and international relations. I feel that any hon. member who read from beginning to end the evidence I have in my hand would feel that in this country we lack facilities. We lack library facilities; we need more scholarships to send students abroad and bring others to us, and I think it is not too much to ask that at some point in Canada we should have a department in a university which could be called "the department of international relations." At the present time we have no such university department. I know as well as other hon. members in this house that we must have economic justice before we can have permanent peace. I realize that education alone will not bring the state I desire. Surely however if we have departments, professors and students who are devoting their time especially to the study of international relations as they exist to-day, we will be doing something to bring about economic justice. It is because this seems to me to be true that I again present the resolution before the house for its favourable consideration. All I ask hon. members to do is to have the resolution again sent to the committee on industrial and international relations.

subtopic: CHAIRS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADLAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest this afternoon to the address which has just been concluded by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). I remember quite well that about a year ago the same hon. member addressed this house upon a motion similar to that to which she has just spoken. The hon. member is to be congratulated on the very deep interest she has always taken in this matter. The subject she has presented to the house is one which must be of general concern to all right thinking people in the various countries of the world; I refer to the great cause of international peace. I realize that it is to that subject she has directed her remarks. If I say sir, that in my humble judgment her proposal is more academic than practical, I trust she will take no offence at my remarks. I think perhaps the motion she has placed before the house may be viewed in the fight of an invitation to engage in a general discussion of the question of the furtherance of peace in the world; that, I take it, is the central idea of her motion. I believe she has in mind more the promotion of peace than a definite proposal for the expenditure of public money in a certain specific manner. One has but to look at the motion and note the exact language of it to form a proper conclusion. The motion is:
That, in the opinion of this house, for every one hundred dollars spent on war one dollar should be spent to promote peace by instituting international professorships and scholarships in leading Canadian universities.

Last year when the matter was under discussion the then Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), now the hon. member for Quebec East, raised an objection which to my mind is very formidable, namely,- that the motion as proposed is contrary to the express provisions of the constitutional act of this country. And I agree with the opinion in that respect expressed last session by the then Minister of Justice. We all realize that in this country we carry on within the confines of a written constitution, and I think we all know that section 93 of that written constitution very definitely prescribes that in and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in regard to education. I know of no section of the British North America Act which is so well known, and so well understood for that matter, as section 93 which I have just quoted, and in my opinion this motion as now drawn and presented to the house contravenes both the letter and the
1456	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Guthrie
spirit of that enactment. Holding that opinion, I for one could not agree that the house accept the motion in its present form.
I do not say for one minute that the constitutional difficulty is insurmountable. I recall many instances during the past fifteen or twenty years in this parliament when we have been able to overcome apparent constitutional difficulties by the manner in which parliament concluded to take action. This motion proposes a straight financial grant of one per cent of the amount which we now spend for armameuts for a special kind of education to be carried on through the agency of certain leading universities in the Dominion. That, in my judgment, Mr. Speaker, is, as I have said, a plain contravention of both the letter and the spirit of the British North America Act. I recall that on many occasions we have been able to circumvent some of the constitutional provisions by which this parliament is surrounded. I recall that this parliament did, on a former occasion, pass legislation to make grants for the construction of highways, and I realize that the question of roads, highways and bridges is purely and simply a question of municipal and of provincial legislation; but we did it, viewing the question of highways as being very closely concerned with the great transportation problems of the Dominion. But we did not do it in the manner suggested in this motion. We did it by a direct grant to the provinces in fair and equitable proportions, and we appointed the provinces the agency for the expenditure and control of that money within certain limitations and conditions which wq attached to, our grant. One need not argue before this house that parliament has no power to engage in ordinary highway construction; but we have power to make grants in aid of it, provided we make our grants through proper agencies and merely in aid of provincial work. So we did, only last August or September, in respect to unemployment- unemployment being a matter primarily municipal, then provincial, and lastly, and only lastly, a matter which pertains to the parliament of Canada; but we made our grants in that case direct to the provinces, and so we were able to overcome any constitutional objections. So we did in regard to technical education. Twenty-five years ago in this house it was urged in some quarters that parliament had no right to spend money upon technical education. I remember very well the discussions which then took place, because I think I had the honour of introducing the first resolution on the question of technical education. At first we thought the most we fMr. Guthrie.]
could do perhaps was to hold an inquiry, and a commission was appointed by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and who was then Minister of Labour, to inquire into the whole question of technical education with the idea of ascertaining just what this parliament could do in regard to the matter. After the report was received parliament did take action, and in spite of section 93 of the British North America Act we made grants to the provinces. Having regard to the population of each province, our grants were upon a fair and equitable basis. We attached certain conditions and limitations to our grants, but we made the provincial authorities the spending authorities and allowed them control of the fund to carry on the great work of technical education within the various provinces.
Now, if such a course were adopted in this motion, I believe the constitutional difficulty would ibe overcome, but a considerable amendment of the motion as it is at present drafted would be required. If this parliament should consider it wise to make grants to further the objects so ably discussed by my hon. friend from Southeast Grey provision might be made for grants of money to the provinces, to be expended by them as they saw fit: but not, I submit, grants to the leading universities. No matter how worthy the object, no matter how good the intent, a grant by this parliament to any of the leading universities for the purposes mentioned in this motion would, I submit, be wholly unconstitutional and beyond the proper legislative sphere of the parliament of Canada. My view in regard to this proposal as it now stands before the house is that upon constitutional grounds it cannot be accepted.
However, there is another side to the question, and very briefly I propose to give the house my own views and opinions thereon.

Then let me say that my hon. friend stated that we had not sufficient peace magazines, peace societies and peace propaganda, and that as compared with other countries we were lacking in that respect. My view, Mr. Speaker-and I have given some considerable thought to the matter-is that of all the countries in the world to-day Canada has been in the forefront in her efforts in support of every movement for the establishment of world peace. That has been the consistent record of this country since the signing of the peace treaty at Versailles in 1919. Other countries may be open to criticism in respect of their efforts in regard to world peace, but of all the countries in the world Canada should be safe from any such criticism.
What is our position in that respect? We are but a small nation numerically; we are not rich. Canada consists of ten million people, at the most, in moderate circumstances, having a tremendous country to care for, yet we were among the first of the nations to subscribe to the peace treaty of Versailles, which was the starting point of all practical peace movements so far as the civilized world is concerned. Likewise we were among the first to subscribe to the covenant of the League o:f Nations, the first great practical measure that ever has been undertaken by the civilized nations to secure the peace of the world. Later
on we were among the first of the nations to subscribe to the theory of the world court, a permanent court of international justice to deal with disputes between nations and to settle those disputes by peaceable means. We subscribed to that at the very first opportunity, and we have adhered to that permanent court throughout all its vicissitudes from -that time down to the present. We have become a party to treaties having to do with the limitation of armament; we have become a party to the treaty for the renunciation of war, and what is more, we were among the first of the nations to accept what is known as the optional clause in regard to submission of all questions of international disputes to the permanent court at The Hague.
It is a strange thing, but within the last ten days no less than three members of this house have asked me just what is that optional clause, and I thought for general information and for convenience it might be well to put it on record. In the treaty under which the permanent court at The Hague is established, there is a clause which nations may aocept or reject. They may sign or they may refuse to sign, but having signed that clause they are compelled to submit practically all international questions to ithe arbitrament and decision of the permanent court. It is a matter of compulsion the moment they have signed the optional clause. Thai clause is as follows:
The undersigned, being duly authorized thereto, further declares on behalf of their government, that, from this date they accept as compulsory ipso facto and without special convention, the jurisdiction of the court in conformity with article 36, paragraph 2, of the statute of the court under the following conditions:
These are the conditions:
The members of the League of Nations and the states mentioned in the annex to the covenant may, either when signing or ratifying the protocol to which the present statute is adjoined or at a later moment, declare that they recognize as compulsory, ipso facto, and without special agreement, in relation to any other member or state accepting the same obligation, the jurisdiction of the court in all or any of the classes of legal disputes concerning:
fa)	The interpretation of a treaty;
fb)	Any question of international law;
(e) The existence of any fact which, if established, would constitute a breach of an international obligation;
(d) The nature or extent of the reparation to be made for the breach of an international obligation.
The declaration referred to above may be made unconditionally or on condition of reciprocity on behaif of several or certain members or states, or for a certain time. In the event of a dispute as to whether the court has jurisdiction, the matter shall be settled by the decision of the court.

International Peace-Mr. Guthrie
Let the house bear in mind that the court was constituted in 1920; its constitution then was settled. That constitution was revised in 1926, and Canada adopted that revised constitution. It was again revised and brought up to date in 1929, and again Canada adopted the revision. Canada has given her consistent support to the establishment of that permanent court for the settlement of international disputes for the last eleven years.
What has been the record of the court? There has been no outbreak of war since its establishment. It has settled case after case of very -far-reaching effect and of very great consequence which, under former conditions, might have resulted in actual hostilities. The record of the court up to date is clear; it is the highest record possible, because we have had no war and we have had no armed outbreaks. The more the nations throughout the world realize the situation and realize what that world court has attained and will attain in the future, I believe the more ready they will be, perhaps all of them, to become parties to the court and to sign the optional clause, as Canada has signed it, as Great Britain has signed it, and as all the British dominions now have signed it.
I grant that the outstanding defect of the permanent court to-day lies in the fact that our great and powerful neighbour to the south has not yet given its complete adherence to that international tribunal. We all hope the day may come, in the not too distant future, when the difficulties will be arranged which at the moment prevent the United States from joining the permanent court and adopting the optional clause. The parties are very close together at this moment, as a matter of fact; the senate of the United States has made five definite reservations, and if these reservations are accepted by the council and by the League of Nations the United States will become a party to the court. Four of these reservations are acceptable already to the League of Nations and to the court; one is still a bone of contention.
I believe most people think that perhaps within the next few months, or within the next year or two, these difficulties will be removed and the United States then will become a full-fledged member of the court and a full signatory to the optional clause, but the United States has lent powerful support to the work of that court and, indeed, to the establishment of the court in its inception. Many of the ablest jurists in the United States have done marvelous work to assist that court. Some of their ablest jurists

have been members of the court, and Mr. Kellogg, the former Secretary of State of the United States, is a member of it to-day, although the United States has not actually accepted the treaty.
The chief aim of that court is, perhaps, the highest aim which the human mind can contemplate: it is peace-international peace, world peace, the avoidance of war, the re-unuciation of war, the abolition of war, with all its dire consequences. Do not think me presumptuous, Mr. Speaker, when I say that the most important policy of this country and of every other country in the world to-day, the most important policy, whether foreign or domestic, is the maintenance of world peace. All other policies fade into insignificance at the merest suggestion of another world conflict. I grant you that it is somewhat discouraging to reflect that during the past year of grace the military and naval armaments throughout the world have increased rather than diminished. They were greater last year than they were prior to the outbreak of the war in 1914. The world's expenditures on naval and military armaments have been, I say, largely increased, notwithstanding leagues and covenants and courts and treaties of limitation, arbitration and renunciation. It only goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that men are not yet willing in this world to beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Something more, perhaps, is required. But that world court is doing all it is humanly possible to do at the moment. It is a practical agency; it is a powerful agency. I doubt whether we could add to its prestige or to its authority or to its power by passing this motion and establishing university scholarships as an aid in the peace movement. Let us devote our energies and our financial aid to those tremendous agencies for peace which are now at work in the world-the League of Nations, with all its ramifications, the permanent court, and the treaties of disarmament, if you will. And that is just another instance in which Canada has shown the world a wonderful example. No one can speak of this countiy as a militaristic country in any sense of the term. True it is that when the occasion arose Canada did herself proud and on short notice raised half a million men to take part in the great conflict. But, I repeat, we are not a militaristic people in any sense of the word. To-day we are the least taxed of any people in the world in regard to military or naval expenditures. I caught a word from the speech of my hon. friend from

International Peace-Mr. Luchkovich
Southeast Grey a moment ago which gave me the impression that she had said we spent about 40 per cent of our budget on armaments.

But it is a proud thing to know that to-day, according to the figures proposed in the estimates laid on the table this session, less than 4 per cent of our budget is for armaments. And if you take our expenditure on the basis of population you will find that this year it will be only $1.65 per head for all the people in Canada-far and away the lowest of any country in the- world. In the United States it is $5.85; in Great Britain, $13.70; in France, $7.60; in Australia, S3.85, and in New Zealand, $3.70, while in Canada, as I say, our expenditure is $1.65 per head for every man, woman and child in the country. Surely Canada is giving the world a real example in the w>ay of disarmament.
I do not say that we should go further in the matter of disarmament. I maintain that we have a trust in this parliament which must be carried out. We are trustees for the people of this country, for the safety of our land, and we must support some armament. Whatever is necessary to safeguard the shores of _ this country from invasion; whatever is necessary for the security of the life and property of our citizens; whatever is necessary to enforce respect for the rights of the people in regard to both life and property; whatever is necessary to maintain peace, order and good government, it is our bounden duty to supply a military force of sufficient strength to see to it that our shores shall remain inviolate, that our population shall be fully protected, and that peace, order and good government shall prevail in this country. I do not believe we can go much lower; indeed, the question that comes up in my mind is whether we have gone down too far already and have cut our estimate too greatly. True it is we have had to have regard to the conditions which prevail financially in Canada during the present year, and the extra cut has become necessary on that account. But I think we all realize that, with the vastness of our possession here, we must provide at least adequate military and possibly naval protection. And that, I am satisfied, this parliament will always grant. At the same time, however, I am glad to be able to state that among all the nations of the world that give returns and statistics
Canada, if judged by the actual figures^ is the least open to censure, the least open to criticism. But I do not think that we should be called upon to spend any more money than we are already spending, especially in academic pursuits such as that proposed in the motion which is now before the house.
Personally I have no objection to this motion going 'back to the committee which dealt with it last year. Much valuable information in regard to the nation seems to have been obtained from the deliberations of that committee. I do not think any practical result can come from the adoption of the motion, and while, as I say, I have no personal abjection to its going before that committee, for my part I think it would be better on all hands if we Simply allowed the matter to drop.

subtopic: CHAIRS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADLAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
I rise to place myself on record as being wholly in accord with the principle of the resolution moved by the hon. lady member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). I rise, firstly, because I am heartily in accord with the purpose of the resolution proposed by the hon. member, and secondly, because I have never before risen to support any lady- that is, on the floor of the House of Commons. In view of the fact that the subject under discussion is the question of peace, I believe it would be in place for me to set an example accordingly , by transposing my reasons for participating in this debate. Thus my chief reason would be to support a lady, especially when she is in such apparent but not real distress owing to the masterly speech delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). And my second reason is my belief in what she says relative to peace.
Realizing as I do that many people in Canada and possibly some hon. members in this house-at least the Minister of Justice has said a few things with respect to what I am going to discuss-might frown upon the proposals made by the hon. lady member, on the ground that they are too purely idealistic, that is to say, righteous in theory but hopeless in practice, as suggested by the Minister of Justice, I should like to offer the Observation that in view of the tremendous necessity of our maintaining civilization, the best minds of the world, including no less a personage than a former prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, are recorded as doing something with respect to peace. Instead of ignoring the peace movement and regarding it as a sort of romantic dream, they are beginning to realize more
1460	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Luchkovich
and more that the peace movement is rooted in common sense and in the fundamental needs of genuine progress. The peace movement is not a mere pipe dream; it is rather the only practical and genuine cure for all the ills that mankind has fallen heir to because of the false and fallacious ideas held by our ancestors with respect to war as a solution for our national and international difficulties.
What great problem has the last war solved? Has it made this world a better, happier and safer place to live in? Who won the war? These are Questions I defy any hon. member to answer effectively and affirmatively. Believing as I do there is no single redeeming or permanently beneficial factor in war 1 cannot see why in the name of heaven we should tolerate or advocate war. The last war proved beyond doubt that there is no such thing as a victor in war; that on the contrary both the vanquished and the supposedly victorious are losers in such a futile conflict. In the words of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, civilization has to end war or war will end civilization. In an address to the World Alliance for International Peace, Mr. Meighen made the following very pertinent remarks:
This race of human beings has to adjust itself to new facts. That is, facts which never existed before. It has to adjust itself to new tremendous facts or pass out. The chief is this; science has given us so great a command over the elements of nature that millions can be snuffed out in this day in a mere matter of moments. Where hundreds fell before in manly contests, arm to arm, great cities, the whole countryside, can now be eaten up by the insatiate man of chemistry.
War has lost its efficacy; it can never bring victory again; it can only bring defeat and despair for both conquerors and conquered; it can leave nothing behind but victors in reaction, and vanquished in revolution, and all alike impoverished. This then is the situation which we face-a long concourse of nations wanting peace, knowing as they must know that a real war now would crush them one and all, drive them back through centuries to primitive poverty and emaciation, until our civilization passes out as did civilization of old, knowing all these things, but nevertheless fearful and arming, ever arming,^ in response to the instinct for security. We know, everybody knows that security by armaments for one country means insecurity for another, and that competitive armaments will end where they have always ended, in competitive war.
What is the conclusion? It is the plainest conclusion ever drawn from the plainest facts. There has to be found a substitute for armaments, something else that will bring security not only to one, but to all. The sovereign right of a single people to fight must yield to the sovereign right of all to live. The practically minded man sees that it means the allocation of forces now controlled by governments, those physical forces which make for 
international destruction, that it means their allocation to abide the judgment of an international congress and their steady reduction to the dimensions of an international police. Let us pray that it does.
I plead again the law of necessity-of imperious overwhelming necessity, for a movement toward this goal is the only substitute for the armament system of this day, a system which left alone, may in no distant time send civilization crashing to its doom.
I doubt whether there is anything in the English language more powerful in its condemnation of war than this excerpt from the speech of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. The remarks which I have just read, coming as they do from a former leader of the party now in power, are perhaps all the more interesting to the house and lend greater force to the resolution which the hon. member for Southeast Grey has this afternoon so eloquently sponsored.
The resolution is a worthy one, deserving the full support of every hon. member. The only criticism I would make of it is not that it goes too far, but rather that it does not go far enough. The resolution as it stands on the order paper would limit the expenditure on the promotion of peace merely to instituting international professorships and scholarships in leading Canadian universities. As I understand the matter, therefore, the young men and women of Canada would not receive the benefit of these peace lectures, or peace propaganda, or whatever you wish to call it, but would have to wait until they matriculated out of high school and entered the university. While I agree that it is better to hear these peace talks even at the advanced age of university entrance than to hear none at all, nevertheless it occurs to me that the best, most effective and proper time to inculcate peace propaganda is when our young men and women are still in the public schools, I believe in the propaganda of peace, but I believe the seeds thereof should be sown in the springtime of youth when the mind is most elastic and receptive. I believe in starting from the bottom up rather than from the top down. That is why I contend that the lessons of peace should commence when children are just beginning to go to school, rather than wait until they are out of public school and high school, and ready to attend the university.
There was a time when it was thought that the only way to get peace was to fight for it, when nations figured that the only way they could be left alone was to make themselves so strong that no one would ever dare to attack them. There were times even in the not too distant past when this opinion

International Peace-Mr. Luchkovich
was considered sound common sense, but as an axiom of international life to-day it has serious drawbacks; for it expresses, as pointed out by Mr. Meighen, in the eyes of the present day intense and extreme nationalism, the main justification for militarism. Therefore, to those of this generation who know but too well to what a pass militarism has brought the world, some alternative to a policy of preparedness, of armed peace, some plan inspired and practical, must present itself instead of the present out of date and bar-borous method of arming for war. I believe the only true alternative is the substitution of the propaganda of peace for the propaganda of war. It includes the consolidation of peace, which consists, on the one hand, in removing as far as possible the causes of war and the preparation of definite means of dealing with situations likely to develop into war. and on the other hand, in the systematic strengthening of international bonds.
I understand that that is the twofold task of the League of Nations, which not only provides the machinery for dealing with the danger of war but, better still, has created a group of institutions the object of which is the strengthening of international friendship and the mutual interdependence of the nations of the world. But there is one force, Mr. Speaker, which it cannot control at will, and on which it must count for the full success of its aims, namely, public opinion, or rather the collective will of each nation to peace, friendship and cooperation with other nations. This end can to some extent be attained by means of the various organs which normally influence public opinion. But the most radical and thorough means of attaining it, the only means that promise deep and lasting results, lie in the education of the younger generation, in the thoughts of peace and the realization of our world citizenship. It is with the latter thought in mind that I refer to the public school as the proper place to start a propaganda of peace. In view of the present curriculum and the various textbooks prescribed I know that it would be a very difficult task for any teacher to do any direct and express teaching on the subject of international peace. But in lieu of a general overhauling and reorientation of our whole educational system, I see no reason why the subject of international peace could not in the meantime be taught in an indirect and incidental manner. There are at least three subjects in conjunction with which it could be taught effectively and efficiently.
Take the subject of history, for instance. In conformity with our modern idea of peace
propaganda, a wider horizon than the history of any particular nation would need to be opened up. Broad notions of world history would need to be given so that the history of one's own particular nation could be seen in its true perspective. I do not mean to say that the standpoint should not be national, for our first concern, after all, is with the land of our birth; but it ought not to be narrowly and exclusively national, for nations may come and nations may go, but the international cosmos goes on forever. History shows us that the Greeks came and the Romans came, and faded away; and that may happen with any civilization, and if the races which war with each other in the older countries would only take cognizance of that fact they would realize wherein lie the seeds of future warfare on the other side of the ocean. I have always thought that there has been too much stress laid on war in our history textbooks, rather than on the progress realized in times of peace. Men like Hannibal and Napoleon are glorified in dozens of pages of our histories while men like Fulton, Stephenson, Faraday and Edison are barely mentioned. Not that history should be falsified in the interests of pacifism by eliminating all mention of wars. Wars certainly are facts of history, and all too significant facts, at that; but war when mentioned must be presented in its true colours, in its cruel and sordid details and its ruinous consequences, somewhat after the fashion of that great book which most hon. members have no doubt read, Journey's End, and that other wellknown book, All Quiet on the Western Front. I can still remember the way I was taught history when I was a young lad. We had to remember the date of every battle and the number of men killed in that battle, and if the fatalities were greater on the enemy side, we thought it quite proper and patriotic to enthuse and gloat over that fact. How we did thrill over the rout and destruction of the enemy! In our youthful experience we were too foolish to understand that the destruction of our enemies meant also the destruction of ourselves. In those days it was considered unpatriotic to think otherwise, so imbued were we with the pernicious war propaganda which even now is so insidiously destroying what is not but should be a paradise on earth. That is one of the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why I support the resolution of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. It is a practical resolution. It is no mere pipe dream, as has already been suggested in this house. On the contrary, it is rooted in common sense and in the fundamental needs of our present-day civilization.

International Peace-Mr. Pouliot
Take the subject of geography. The teacher is afforded here an almost equally good opportunity for instruction in sane internationalism. Full advantage should be taken of the new and better methods of teaching the subject, of laying stress on international links at all times, on international communications of all kinds, international commerce and industry, and migration. The growing internationalism of science and sport might also be referred to incidentally. Look at the way the world has been brought closer together by means of railways, steamships, aeroplanes, radio and moving pictures. But facts of this kind will not produce the desired effect unless their significance is brought out. Think of the thrill of the first aeroplane flight across the Atlantic from Europe that was made together by a Britisher and a German. How vastly different and more humane was it than the murderous struggle between the British and German nations that took place in the- great world war of 1914. It should also be shown that the different countries of the world are becoming to an ever-increasing extent dependent upon one another, and that all this international life is dislocated by war, in which ordinary men and women suffer in countless numbers.
Finally there is the religious aspect of peace. That is too delicate a subject for a layman like myself to discuss, and I therefore leave it to the more competent care and inspired guidance of the great spiritual leaders of the world.
I know that the hon. member for Southeast Grey will pardon me for digressing from the resolution as it is worded on the order paper, because I feel confident that she will agree with everything I have so far said on this subject. Her resolution calls for a specific expenditure out of the Dominion treasury for a specific purpose, namely, that, "for every one hundred dollars spent on war one dollar should be spent to promote peace by instituting international professorships and scholarships in leading Canadian universities". While that does not include the whole gamut of human relationships from public school to the universities, nevertheless it would ultimately tend to reach our young boys and girls. Be that as' it may, I am sure that the main purpose of the mover is to eliminate the propaganda of war and to substitute for it the propaganda of peace. For that reason I am going to support the spirit of the resolution, the discussion of which I hope will be. facilitated if it is referred to a committee. I now move an amendment to that end:
That the motion be amended by inserting after the word "house" the following: "the

government take into consideration that"; and inserting after the word "peace" the words: "and that such an amount be granted to the provinces for the purpose of"; and by deleting the word "by" in line three; and adding to the motion the words: "and that this motion be referred to the committee on industrial and international relations for consideration and to report to this house."

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temiscouata):	Mr. Speaker, in the first place I
wish most heartily to congratulate the mover (Miss Macphail). Often it has been said that our lady colleague represents the women of this country, and this. resolution proves the truth of that statement. There is no woman in Canada who would not be favourable to it. It says:

At present some money is spent by this country to help make possible the promotion of peace by the' League of Nations. Some people may think that the league will provide a utopia. True, its results are not always apparent, but it gives an opportunity to the people of every race, creed and nation to meet together at Geneva to discuss international problems of wide importance. As these people meet together at different intervals, it is possible for them to discuss together matters of common interest.
Some years ago in the New York Times an article was published by Marshal Foch to the effect that the next war would be the most terrible and the most disastrous in the history of the world. Warfare has gone from bad to worse, and science is all the time studying new means of destroying human beings and property. With the innovation of powerful aeroplanes, mighty dirigibles which cross oceans and continents, and bombs more

International Peace-Mr. LaVergne
destructive than any hitherto devised, a city the size of New York, London or Paris might be destroyed within a few hours. In to-night's issue of the Evening Citizen appears the following statement concerning a riot in Spain:
Mob applies torch to Catholic buildings in anti-church outbreak.
This is only one instance of what has happened in Europe, despite the excellent work of the League of Nations and the good will of the leaders of every state.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Leaders of democracy.

speechtext:
I am a firm believer in
democracy; it has done a great deal of good in promoting the welfare of humanity.

speechtext:
One cannot always prevent crazy or greedy people from waging riots and wars; therefore everything should be done to promote peaceful relationships among nations.
If the house agrees to the resolution, I suggest that a part of the money be applied to the teaching of Canadian history in Canadian schools. How can we be proud of our country if we have not learned the history of our forefathers? In fact the history of Canada is one of the most interesting histories of any country in the world. The work of the pioneers and its continuance by their successors until Canada has reached its present stage of development should be taught to our children in the primary schools. Sometimes this teaching is not as complete as it should be. My hon. friend from Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovrch) suggested that part of the grant should be given to the provinces. That might well be done to encourage the provinces to promote the teaching of the history of Canada in the primary schools.

speechtext: Have the provinces asked for it?

If they have not, why not bring the matter up at the next interprovincial conference? It is a matter of the utmost importance.
Mr. LaVERGNE: It is not a very peaceful history.

speechtext:
But it is a history that records very few riots,-except lately the Quebec riots, which were rather justified. The times were not peaceful when the French settlers had to fight the Indians who were massacring the first missionaries-the first propagandists of civilization in this country. Nor were the times peaceful when they had to fight to preserve Canada to the British crown. But, as my friend knows, French-Can-adians stood for the British connection in 1775 and 1812, in spite of the fact that they were invited by Montgomery to join the Americans in their war against Great Britain.
Mr. LaVERGNE: If my memory is good, they had a few fights with the British crown before that.

subtopic: CHAIRS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADLAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Yes; but not afterwards. With the exception of 1837. Certainly Canadians had to fight for their rights. For instance, Lafontaine fought in the. legislative chamber for the French language, but- he used constitutional means in fighting for and preserving our rights. To-day Canada has become a nation. We are proud of it. This position could not be attained at once on account of the old racial prejudices that existed, but little by little those prejudices have been overcome, Canada has asserted her rights, and to-day she is one of the most-admired nations of the world. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, while it is impossible to prevent war, any steps that will delay such a catastrophe must be favoured and supported by every right thinking citizen in this country.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montma-gny): Mr. Speaker, if I could see any good reason to become a feminist it would be in the debating ability of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). She has certainly shown equality in debate of woman with man, although I do not know whether I am paying her a very high compliment in saying that.

subtopic: CHAIRS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADLAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
I am not so sure.
Mr. LaVERGNE: But, as I indicated to my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pou-liot), I am not such a rabid believer in democracy. There is an old proverb, almost as old as civilization itself, which tells us, "Si vis pacem, para bellum,"-if you want peace, prepare for war. I should like to support the motion if I understood exactly what it meant.
-for every one hundred dollars spent on war one dollar should be spent to promote peace-
1464	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. LaVergne
Everyone agrees with that. But how can we do it? And how can we come to a balancing of accounts? In my opinion the motion goes back about 170 years for its inspiration; it goes back to Jean Jacques Rousseau, who believed in the inborn goodness of man, that man was born good but that ci vlization or society had made him bad; which I think is contrary to the doctrine of original sin; for I have been taught that man is born evil and that it is only by redemption that he can become good. As a result of the theories of Jean Jacques Rousseau and Voltaire we had the French revolution. About a year before the king of France was beheaded all the members of the French national assembly were kissing one another in the belief that the revolution had ushered in the era of eternal peace and eternal goodness. Then the poor king, who through weakness or lack of knowledge of human nature, had accepted those theories, was beheaded. For the next fifteen or twently years Europe was in a state of almost continual war. Then we had that great-great-grandfather of the League of Nations, La Sainte alliance-the Holy Alliance-which was to preserve eternal peace in Europe, and this practically meant world peace. We know what happened. France had to defend herself against three invasions culminating in the siege of Paris by the Prussians in 1870, which was followed by the worst condition of all, the destruction of France by Frenchmen fighting against one another.
My opinion, if it is worth anything, is that the best way to prepare for peace is to build up a strong nation, to get citizens in their youth to believe in their duty to their country-not to humanity as a whole. Serve your country and you will be serving humanity. Give everything you have, your thoughts, your will, your talents, your future, your whole soul to your country, and you will be doing more for the peace of the world than by believing in international doctrines, doctrines which have produced what we see in Russia to-day-starvation, the negation of civilization, of the belief in God, of the belief in everything that humanity has always held sacred. Of course, I may appear to some of my hon. friends as very backward, but two thousand years ago we were told in the Sermon on the Mount: "All things whatsoever ye would that men should do unto you, do ye even so to them." But even if you do believe in this doctrine yourself, it is impossible to get the other party to believe in it too. Suppose the whole of Canada were disarmed and we said:	We believe in
[Mr. LaVergne. 1
absolute peace; the peace of all humanity. We believe humanity is good; we are going to throw away all armaments; we are going to do away with all military education. We will do away with police, because we believe the people will stop robbing and stop murdering. As a great Frenchman said, with regard to the abolition of capital punishment, "Que messieurs les assassins commencent," or, "Let the murderers begin." Suppose Canada believed in this principle; could we be sure the other nations of the world would believe in it? What was the result in Belgium in 1914, a country whose neutrality was guaranteed by the great powers of Europe' The neutrality of Belgium was violated by Germany, a country which had signed the treaty of neutrality. Two years later the same people who had denounced the violation of the neutrality of Belgium were violating the neutrality of Greece; I refer to France and England. These are very lofty, idealistic sentiments, but they never will become anything more while human nature remains what it is.

subtopic: CHAIRS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADLAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
Might I ask the
hon. gentleman what he would do with the League of Nations, which is perhaps one of the most idealistic institutions in the world to-day?
Mr. LaVERGNE: That is a hard question to ask me-what I would do with the League of Nations, which is only a repetition of the Holy Alliance of 1815. I believe the League of Nations is doing its very best, but I sincerely believe the League of Nations cannot stop war. I believe that the day Russia is prepared, as she is preparing now, she will jump on the nations of Europe and America in an attempt to force upon them her theories of utopia and her new civilization, if it may be so called, by means of war.
It is quite impossible to believe that war will ever disappear, after all the years of human history. That is my conviction. I may be wrong; I hope that some day we will have a world-although I am afraid we shall not see it-where humanity will believe in peace and charity, but that cannot be and will not be until the teachings of the Master, who came to this world two thousand years ago, are accepted. Two thousand years have passed; those teachings are not acoepted as yet, and I am afraid it will be a very long time before they are accepted.
In conclusion, my theory is this: If you want to build up peace for our country and for the world, build up citizens who believe in their country and in their duty to their country, who believe that their first duty is to give their life to their country. In my opinion

International Peace-Miss Macphail
there is no greater movement in this direction and no surer way of accomplishing it than by building up our cadet movement all through Canada. In that way our children will be taught not only high ideals but also discipline. They will be taught to believe in authority; they will be taught that their lives do not belong to them only but to their country. This brings me back to the history of Canada, to which my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) referred. I despise and hate the word French-Canadian.

subtopic: CHAIRS AND SCHOLARSHIPS IN CANADLAN UNIVERSITIES TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL UNDERSTANDING AND GOOD WILL
speechtext:
What is wrong with it?
Mr. LaVERGNE: We are not French-Oana-dians; we are Canadians and nothing else. We are Canadians who speak French, but we were Canadians under the French regime and we shall not be hyphenated by anybody in this country. The history of us Canadians of French descent and of French language is not peaceful. Our ancestors were warriors. They believed that they owed to their country, to their forefathers and to their children the only grant which God has given man, which is life. You can preach on any doctrine; can you do away with sorrow in this world? You cannot. As you live you will see your dear ones disappear and you cannot do away with the sorrow which you feel by any social law or legislation. Can you do away with sickness by passing an act of parliament? If you can I will be the first to support the bill. Can you do away with death? You cannot. We should not forget that this life is only a passage, a transition. All sorrows, all misfortunes, mean nothing in the great scheme of things. The Russians teach that religion is only opium for the people, but it is a mighty good opium in that final operation of death. Unless we believe we must fight for our traditions, any social legislation is absolutely useless.
In closing let me say this: I believe that if we want to prepare for peace we dhould prepare for war. Let us build up a strong nation; let us build up our cadet movement and put in the minds of our young people the thought that we are trying to build up citizens who will believe in discipline, in authority and in something higher than the selfishness of mankind. I remember when I was quite a young iman, as a young officer following a course, hearing a lecture by an Australian officer.

They would be rude; they would do anything. After the introduction of compulsory service the change in the youth of Australia was remarkable. I believe .there is no better education for the young man than a military education. He is taught the idea of discipline; he is taught respect and those higher things a citizen owes to his country. speechtext:
It will take me only a moment or so to say what I wish to say. I was very much disappointed in the speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) this afternoon. Does the minister suppose I did not know, and that other members of the house did not know, the different things which have been done by the government of Canada and by other nations to bring about peace in the world? I may tell him that I am as familiar with them as he is. It is because the government does these things with which the people of Canada are not familiar, that I feel the need of further educational facilities, that the young people may get a thorough training in the international relations into which Canada has entered. If, as the Minister of Justice has said, we have taken first place in the world-'which I very much doubt-it would be a very good thing to keep that place. And that is all the more reason why we should have some education. The government of last year had a different way of getting out of the difficulty, although, of course, both governments successfully got out. But I must say, in fairness to the late Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that his methods are niter. I do not think that the present Minister of Justice is informing the house correctly when he says that the Department of National Defence give their money to the province and
1456	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macphail
the province distributes it here and there for cadet training. That is not exactly true. I have here an extract from the minutes of the Board of Education, Toronto, of March 5, 1931, in which this statement appears:
That the sum of $200, received from the Department of National Defence as a result of two former pupils of Danforth branch technical school having enlisted in the permanent air force after taking a two years' course at Camp Borden, be appropriated to the credit of the school for orchestra requirements.
I have nothing more to say. There is no reason why I should excite mysef regarding the education of Canadian youth in Canadian universities any more than one other hon. member. I believe, as the four witnesses last year and the three professors Who wrote us, made perfectly clear, that there is need of greater facilities.
The Minister of Justice suggested that Canada was looking to new ways of ensuring security and peace. If that is true, then the Dominion government has jurisdiction so far as the method of bringing about that condition is concerned, just as it had jurisdiction in the sphere of armaments. I must say I wa3 not impressed with the hon. gentleman's speech. I did not think he made clear any real objection to the motion except on the ground of its wording, which I admit is poor. I see no reason why the house should not send the resolution to the committee, though I admit, in view of the statement of the leader of the government that they do not approve of it, its reference to the committee will not help very much. We know that government members are in the majority on committees and we know also, in spite of all the talk about democracy, that the government governs. All that the rest of us can do is talk, which I do not propose to do at greater length at the moment.
