subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that Canada should have the right to amend her own constitution, but that in proceeding to make any amendment, scrupulous care should be taken to safeguard the rights of minorities.
He said: At the recent conference between the Dominions and the provinces re the proposed statute of Westminster we find that the subject matter of this resolution was under discussion. I might say that that conference in itself was without precedent and perhaps created a rather dangerous precedent, although I frankly admit that the results were very satisfactory. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has promised another conference to consider amendments to the British North America Act, so that it would seem opportune that the house should discuss the Whole question.
When I introduced a resolution along this line some seven years ago, I was attacked on two sides. The imperialists, on the one hand, accused me of wanting to cut the. painter by which we were bound to the motherland. Their objection has been largely silenced by the Imperial conference itself of 1926, in which we heard such statements as "autonomous communities" and "equal in status and in no way subordinate one to another". On the other hand, at that time the guardians of provincial rights were up in arms. They considered that our British connections were safeguarding minority rights, and that objection is still to the fore although it comes from Ontario rather than from Quebec. Of this, more a little later.

British North America Act
I frankly recognize that any difficulty that confronts us is not at Westminster but here in Canada. The British parliament will undoubtedly meet Canada's views in this regard. We in Canada must come to an agreement. On the other hand, there is not much doubt that [DOT] the existing situation is an excuse for inaction. So long as we think we have to go overseas to settle the matter, it is very easy for either the Dominion or the provinces to blame their lack of action upon the British North America Act.
It is practical considerations that lead me to introduce this amendment. Social legislation of almost every kind is blocked by the British North America Act. Further than that, we cannot carry out our obligations under the Versailles treaty until we have some blearer understanding of the relative jurisdiction of the Dominion and the provinces. There are a number of questions to be bleared up. First of all, there is the question: what amendments are needed? Then as to procedure-and this is one of the most knotty problems-there is the question: how can these amendments be secured? Again there is the whole question of what the United States people call constitutional limitations, that to which I have referred in the resolution itself when I urge that in proceeding to make any amendment we should see that scrupulous care is taken to safeguard the rights of minorities, a suggestion in which-whatever amendments are made- I believe every hon. member will fully concur.
I propose for a few minutes to give a brief survey of the situation as it exists to-day, also some of the anomalies with which we wrestle. Since confederation there have been before the courts not less than five hundred constitutional cases. Supposing we place the average cost at $5,000 a case, which I take it would be a very moderate estimate, the house can see that millions of dollars are involved in litigation of this kind. Only the lawyers benefit, and I would suggest to my lawyer friends to-night that some of them at least should be sufficiently patriotic to support this resolution and thus place the interests of the country at large ahead of their own pecuniary advantage.
There are questions relative to geographical boundaries. In the old, simple agricultural communities, it was comparatively easy to set up line fences, and when the fathers of confederation were drawing up the British North America Act, that is what was done. They simply said: here are certain things that come within the boundaries of the provinces. But the problem is not quite so easy in the more complicated life of to-day. For example, who owns the air? The old scripture says "The wind bloweth where it listeth," but Premier Taschereau says that Quebec owns the air over Quebec. The question arises:	What about flying in the air? The
supreme court states that the Dominion does not possess exclusive authority with regard to control of aviation, but that the provinces have some rights. There we begin to get into difficulties. So with radio regulations. That question is now before the Supreme Court of Canada. Then there comes the whole question of water powers. It is easy to stake the land; it is not so easy to stake, as it were, the water. Take the question of the St. Lawrence river, which is certainly a knotty problem. The St. Lawrence river is part of a great system of waterways, extending from the great lakes to the Atlantic; it has not only interprovincial connections, but also international relations. Therefore it is not so easy to say just who should control a great stream like that, or the hydro powers that may be generated on it. Let me remind the house that some years ago, there was some difficulty with regard to the head waters of the rivers that supplied power for Manitoba. To meet the situation certain water powers in Ontario were placed under Dominion control. This was done under that clause in the British North America Act which refers to such works as are declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada.
Take another question, the fisheries in British Columbia. It used to be that fisheries clearly came under Dominion control, but now in the processing of fish we find that the canneries have to be erected on the land, and hence it was discovered that the Dominion had not exclusive control and was not in a position to grant certain licenses. Life to-day is much more complicated than it was sixty years ago.
Take other matters that relate to what might be called the boundaries with regard to certain political relations. The supreme court, for example, a few years ago decided that a woman was not a person within the meaning of the British North America Act. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has evidently amended our constitution by what someone has termed judicial legislation. The British North America Act is regarded by their lordships as "a living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits." Let me say with regard to that position that in the Canadian Bar review Mr. George F. Henderson, K.C. of Ottawa, has given us .a very interesting and incisive comment. He says:
If, having regard to considerations of political expediency and the welfare of the state, the statute can be construed in accordance with
British North America Act

legal principles, so much the better, but, if not, those principles must yield to "the larger view" which political exigency dictates, the semblance of an observance of legal canons being given to the opinion delivered in order not too greatly to shock those who pin their faith to His Majesty the king in council as the final court of appeal for all countries of the British commonwealth except England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
There are other matters which have not been quite so satisfactorily settled, and about which we still have a good deal of trouble. I shall briefly enumerate some of them.
Take the question of the troops that were sent down to Nova Scotia in 1925. Who was to pay the bill? That question was before the courts, and I do not know that it has been decided yet.
Then there was the question of soldiers operating cars in New Brunswick without licence-again a question involving Dominion and provincial control.
There is the question of taxation. The provinces, we all know, are restricted to direct taxation, and yet the gasoline tax, which a good many of our provinces have put into operation, comes dangerously near being an indirect tax.
Again, can liquor legally purchased in Quebec be brought into Ontario? Liquor to be purchased legally in Ontario, under the Liquor Control Act, must be bought from the government vendor. Liquor may be legally sold in Quebec, but that same liquor cannot be legally bought in Ontario.
Again, the right of the Dominion to control the manufacture of liquor is still an open question.
Take the question that we had up no later than this afternoon, when my hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) was urging that a grant should be made to promote peace. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) takes the ground that it is quite within the competence of the Dominion government to make war and to foster the cadet movement, even although that means going into our schools; but it is quite outside our powers to do anything that will foster peace. You can see, Mr. (speaker, the difficulties into which this British North America Act is driving us.
Take another realm altogether, that of trade and commerce. In the old days, sixty years ago, trade was very largely local in character, and it was very easy to control it. But now under the British North America Act we have no definite line of demarcation with regard to the incorporation and licensing of companies. Let me give a few illustrations, which will be familiar to legal gentlemen at all events. The John Deere Plow case of 1913 established that 
a federal charter entitled the company to do business in the province and to resist many forms of provincial control. That was a blow at provincial control. On the other hand, the Bonanza Creek case, in 1915, established that a provincial charter under the British North America Act entitled a company to enter other provinces-a blow at federal control. Later, we had the legality of the British Columbia Produce Marketing Act challenged, and the act partly destroyed. We have had a dispute with regard to the Canada Grain Act. We have had our Old Age Pension Act of 1926 disputed by Quebec, although the question has never been carried to the courts. The British Columbia Minimum Wage Act was challenged. The Combines Investigation Act was challenged, and has recently been sustained. The Live stock and Live Stock Products Act, as far as it relates to grading, is really ultra vires of the Dominion parliament, and there has to be enabling legislation on the part of the provinces. The licensing and control of insurance companies is being protested by the province of Ontario. Some hon. gentlemen who were on the Banking and Commerce Committee a few years ago can remember the representations that were made in that regard. The Manitoba Sale of Shares Act has ben declared invalid. Concerning this Toronto Saturday Night of October 26, 1928, said very bitterly:
The privy council has decided that the provinces have no control over a rotten company so long as it is for the general advantage of Canada.
Now I come to the questions in which I am more particularly concerned; that is, matters relating to social legislation. Take the Canada Temperance Act; it is not at all clear as to where the jurisdiction lies. The Lord's Day Act has been challenged, and as a matter of fact it is put into operation in some of the provinces in a rather peculiar fashion.
Mr. LaVERGNE: That is settled by the act itself.

speechtext:
I know, but they
were treading on such thin ice that they had to make some very special arrangements, and some of my lawyer friends tell me that it is not very good law when it is done in that fashion. '
There is the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The privy council in 1925 when it upset the validity of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, in discussing the question of Russell vs. the Queen, had this to say:
It appears to thedr lordships that it is not now open to them to treat Russell vs. the Queen as having established the general principle that

British North America Act
the mere fact that Dominion legislation is for the general advantage of Canada or is such that it will meet a mere want which is felt throughout the Dominion renders it competent if it cannot be brought within the heads enumerated specifically in section 91.
I am not very familiar with these various decisions, but it strikes me that their lordships found it very hard to get over the Canada Temperance Aot, which had been held to be within the power of the Dominion parliament. The judges took the view, and to me this is positively funny, that intemperance at that time was so greait as to be, in their words anational calamity. . . . An epidemic of pestilence might conceivably be regarded as analogous. It is plain from the decision of the board of commerce case that the evil of profiteering could not have been so invoked; for provincial powers, if exercised, were adequate to it.
Now I come to the even more important question, and that is of our responsibility under the Versailles treaty arid the draft conventions subsequent thereto. Take the question of the minimum wage. We had that question before our select standing committee on industrial and international relations, and in the report of 1926 I read this:
It was stated by the Deputy Minister of Justice that according to the British North America Act legislative jurisdiction in regard to minimum wages is vested primarily in the provincial legislatures.	.
He also quoted section 132 of the British North America Act as follows:
The parliament of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or any provinces thereof us part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries, arising out of any treaty between the empire and such foreign countries.
Commenting on this he said:
There can be no doubt that where Canada has entered into am obligation by treaty-and in that connection I mean an association within the empire, of course-within the meaning of section 132 which I have just read-I do not think there is any doubt but that parliament has power to legislate for the purpose of carrying into effect the provision of the treaty.
The report concludes with these very significant words:
_ This opinion goes to show that the British North America Act by no means contemplates industrial problems of the kind and scope to which Canadians to-day must adjust themselves.
That seems to be a very fair statement of the situation in which we find ourselves. Sixty years ago life was comparatively simple. At that time there was no labour movement and very little industrial development. No one had foreseen the great European
war; no one knew that there would be an international labour office established and that we would seek the world over to standardize labour. No one realized any of these things. And so although the British North America Act may have admirably fitted conditions as they were at the time it was enacted, it falls far short of meeting the needs with which we are faced to-day. I would like once more to read that section of the report:
^This opinion goes to show that the British North America Act by no means contemplates industrial problems of the kind and scope to which Canadians to-day must adjust themselves.
I go on to note that although apparently it is impossible for us to pass a Minimum Wage Act in the Dominion, the Minimum Wage Act of British Columbia, a piece of provincial legislation, was declared ultra vires,
I wish now to go to the question of unemployment insurance, which during the last two or three sessions has been so much before the house. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, a committee of this house was appointed to deal with that matter. The industrial and international relations committee report of 1928 referred to a report from the Minister of Justice, 1921, P.C. 2722:
In this view unemployment insurance has a pronounced federal aspect and on the whole the minister thinks the establishment of a system of unemployment insurance is competent to the Dominion in the exercise of its residuary legislative power with relation to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
Yet that committee reported that it was impossible for the Dominion to do anything about unemployment insurance. The other day the Prime Minister from his seat promised this house and the country that his government would enact a measure of unemployment insurance. At least that was the meaning which a good many hon. members took from his words; that was the meaning which the press spread abroad throughout the country. I understand that in some quarters there may be question about that matter, but it does seem to me that the Prime Minister ought not to allow so important a statement to be ambiguous. Hon. members should know very clearly what he meant. I would point out, however, that if we are to accept the report of the committee of this house appointed a year or two ago it is impossible for the Prime Minister to carry out his promise. What does the report say? I quote:
That the evidence of the Justice department makes it clear that the responsibility for such legislation rests on the provincial authorities, it being within their jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act, but that it would be within the power of par-

British North America Act

liament to contribute by grant to such provinces as adopted such legislation following the precedent set in the matter of technical education, highway construction, and, more recently, the Old Age Pensions Act.
Then, there is the question of the eight hour day. According to a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada:
The subject matter is generally within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces, but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the Dominion government or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province.
I think in view of the very hurried survey I have given of the actual situation which confronts Canada to -day that the ordinary man at least can realize the need for a change and for some qualifying amendments.
Two years ago I was invited to present this subject before the Canadian Club of Montreal. I accepted the invitation with some trepidation, because I thought I might have difficulty in persuading the people of Montreal in the province of Quebec to accept my proposal for changes in the British North America Act. To my delight, however, I found that a large number of them were tremendously interested in the question, and from the practical standpoint they were convinced of the need of bringing about these changes. They did not seem to see all the difficulties which some legal gentlemen in this house seem constantly to find.
Conditions are not static. Hon. members will recall that Alice in Wonderland-or was it the Queen-said:
You must run very fast if you would keep where you are.
I believe that to be absolutely true. Conditions are sweeping along very rapidly and we must keep advancing if we are to keep relatively in the same place, to say nothing of making advances. Acts must be changed in the letter if we would keep the spirit.
Further than that may I suggest if our forefathers had brains enough to devise a constitution to meet the needs of their day we should have brains enough to revise it to meet the needs of our day. Some of us revere the British North America Act as the laws of the Medes and Persians that cannot change. Let me urge: If we are not impotent, let us be the fathers of something. The fathers of confederation differed from the men about them in that they were willing to take a chance on a change. A precedent is merely the method by which someone makes an

escape from an impossible situation. It is time we set a few precedents in this house.
I have not time to discuss the legislation of other dominions, but I would simply remark they have the right to amend their constitutions; why has not Canada a similar right? Either we are a nation or we are not a nation. If we are a nation we should have the right to change our constitution. We hear a great deal about provincial rights. I suggest to the house that the fear of the minorities is not healthy. Their belief in the help that can come from Great Britain is entirely illusory, and I think the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who unfortunately is not here tonight has come to accept that fact. I read from the proceedings of the Imperial conference the following statement:
Every self governing member of the empire is now master of its own destiny.
We should accept the position to which we have now attained. We are told that the provinces should be consulted. Should they all agree before action is taken? That of course is another question. At the Imperial conference it was decided in regard to the West-(minster Act that the ratification off the proposed act would be in the hands of the British government by August 1, 1931. The report of the conference of 1930 declared:
To this end it seemed desirable to place on record the view that the sections of the statute relating to the Colonial Laws Validity Act should be so drafted as not to extend to Canada unless the statute was enacted in response to such requests as are appropriate to an amendment of the British North America Act.
The conference did not explain what it meant by the phrase, "as are appropriate to an amendment." The Prime Minister was reported to have declared that the approval of the nine Canadian provinces would be necessary to ratification. The Montreal Gazette observed that consulting the provinces did not necessarily imply that their consent was essential. Up to this time the Prime Minister has been entirely and perhaps discreetly silent on this point. Apparently he yielded to the influence of Mr. Ferguson, who stated explicitly in the concluding paragraph of his memorandum issued just before the conference :
It is therefore earnestly represented that no restatement of the procedure for amending the constitution of Canada can be accepted by the province of Ontario that _ does not fully and frankly acknowledge the right of all the provinces to be consulted and to become parties to the decisions arrived at.
I would ask hon. members to note the words, "right of all the provinces". Here we come to the treaty or compact theory of

British North America Act
confederation, and I suggest that since this is purely a legal matter it must be met more or less by legal argument. Let me ask, what provinces gave consent? There were at that time only three provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Canada, because we were still operating under the Act of Union of 1840. It is very doubtful if Quebec or Ontario could be said to have given consent, for they were then part of the province of Canada.
Further than that, what do we mean by the provinces? Do we mean the electorates? In New Brunswick the electorate were in favour of the principle of confederation, but they never pronounced on the London resolutions or the British North America Act. In Nova Scotia there was no chance for them to pronounce on anything before the British North America Act was passed; then they were opposed to it.
Do you mean the legislatures? Canada approved the Quebec resolutions but prorogued before the appointment of delegates to the London conference, and therefore could not approve the British North America Act before it was passed. New Brunswick authorized the appointment of delegates to the London conference but prorogued before the conference, and met again only after the British North America Act was passed. Nova Scotia authorized the appointment of delegates to the London conference and was the only one approving the reference after the British North America Act was passed. Prince Edward Island and British Columbia assented to the terms of union. There were no legislatures, of course, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta until they were created by the Dominion parliament.
Did the governments consent? These did consent, except, of course, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Then we come to the other question that is more important: What is the pact to which reference is made? Was it the Quebec resolutions? These were approved by the legislature of Canada only, and by no electorate. Was it the London resolutions? These were not approved by any of the legislatures until after the British North America Act Was passed. In seven important matters the British North America Act differed from the Quebec resolutions. The British North America Act was not thus approved. The situation is well summarized by Mr. John S. Eiwart:
A statute arranged not in Canada but in England by delegates from Canada who, although bound by the Quebec resolutions, departed widely from them; by delegates from
Nova Scotia who were known not to represent Nova Scotia's wishes; and the proceedings purposely kept secret from the people who might by "reverberation" of it be "stirred to its depths" in opposition, can hardly be regarded as a contract.
And what procedure has actually been followed in obtaining these changes in the pact? I might say in passing that the reports of the debates are very illuminating. There is no support whatever for the contentions of the advocates of provincial rights, and the fathers of confederation who participated in these debates supported the changes by dominion action. Take the changes brought about by the Imperial parliament. In 1871 power was given to the Dominion parliament to create provinces. The act was passed on an address of both houses of the D|ominion parliament; the provinces were not consulted. In 1875 an act regarding the privileges of parliament was passed on the request of the Dominion cabinet only. In 1886 plenary power was granted to the Dominion parliament to provide for the representation of territories in both houses. This was passed on an address of the two bouses. In 1895 power was granted, to the Dominion parliament to provide fora deputy speaker for the Senate. This was-passed on an address by the Dominion parliament. In 1907 the change in regard to provincial subsidies was passed on an address of the two houses. Let me point out that the provinces were consulted for the first time on-this occasion. British Columbia protested and: secured only a slight verbal modification, lit 1915 a change was made with regard to additional senators from the west. This act also was passed on an address of the two houses, but the provinces were not consulted. In 1916 an imperial act dealing with the prolongation of the life of parliament was passed on a joint address of the two houses only. Last year the legislation for the return of the natural resources to the western provinces, as every hon. member will recall, was passed on the joint address of both houses, and only the western provinces were consulted. We must come to this conclusion, that in these eight acts the provinces were consulted only once,, in 1907, and then did not give unanimous consent.
Now take the changes made by the Canadian parliament itself. At least nine acts changing the financial basis of confederation were passed, and on these the provinces were never consulted.
I should like to point out that the basis of confederation has changed a great deal since
im
British North America Act

1S67. Judicial decisions have fundamentally changed the balance of legislative power, and for this I suppose, the late Lord Haldane was very largely responsible. There have been other developments which I can only enumerate; development of Canada's diplomatic service; appointment of the Governor General on the sole advice of the Dominion cabinet; separate negotiation and signature of treaties; membership in the League of Nations and on its council. The provinces were not consulted in any of these changes-changes which were much more important than many of the little things about which we make so much fuss.
Let me point out the effects of the theory that unanimous consent is necessary. Take the situation of the three western provinces. Is their consent needed? Then that is giving an altogether fictitious character to these provinces, and it is as if a child were supposed to ratify a contract which had been made long before he was born. Is the consent of these western provinces not needed? Then I, as representing one of these provinces, would be the first to protest, because we in the west have as much right, at the present day, as .any of the eastern provinces to be consulted.
If the unanimous consent of all the provinces is required there would be an inevitable tendency towards constitutional rigidity. This point I have not time to develop, nor have I the time to speak of the danger of the minority being given power to override the majority. We a,re here approaching the fundamental question of sovereignty. Mr. R. K. Finlayson, writing in the Free Press of December 8, 1928, gave this warning:
It required the Civil war to prove to the individual states of America that it is not the part of individual states to challenge the authority of the union by a sovereignty written into a piece of paper.
The trouble is that we think altogether too much in legal terms. The British North America Act is not altogether a contract. May I suggest that it more nearly resembles what marriage is according to the Roman Catholic idea as I understand it; it is much nearer to being something at a sacrament. The union has gone on for years, children are involved, and the parties must learn to rub along somehow.
The former Minister of Justice, at the Dominion-provincial conference of 1927, spoke of one procedure that might be followed in amending the British North America Act. He proposed that there should be different classes of questions dealt with in different ways. He said:
In order that adequate safeguards should be provided it was proposed that in the event

of ordinary amendments being contemplated the provincial legislatures should be consulted, and a majority consent of the provinces obtained, while in the event of vital and fundamental amendments being sought involving such questions as provincial rights, the rights of minorities, or rights generally affecting race, language and creed, unanimous consent of the provinces should be obtained.
.... In view of the present usage of automatic acceptance of proposals made and of the practice in all the other dominions, the minister contended that it would be better if in the future amendments to the British North America Act should be made by legislation of the Dominion parliament, subject to the conditions set forth. The questions on which unanimity of the provinces should be required might be specified under sections 93 and 133 and section 92, subsections 12, 13 and 14 of the British North America Act.
These sections refer to education, language, property and civil rights and administration of justice. I should like to suggest an alternative procedure. The Commonwealth of Australia has its constitutional act containing eight general clauses. Then follows the constitution, and so the rights of minorities might be recognized in our contemplated constitutional act. That is, there would be what the Americans call certain constitutional limitations. These would be clearly set forth in the preamble, and then we would be in a position to modify as long as we did not infringe upon these fundamental rights, which would be those now recognized under the British North America Act.
I take it that what we need before long is a constitutional conference. The Prime Minister has already promised that, but as I said, I am not at all sure that we can concede that all the provinces should be satisfied. As a practical measure I suppose it would be a good thing to call all the provinces into consultation, but certainly whatever the provinces may have to put forward, it does seem to me that the federal parliament should know what amendments it wants from its standpoint, and that means careful study and discussion.
I should like to close by urging again, as I did in the beginning, the pressing need for clarifying amendments. I urge that we should have the right to amend, recognizing that after all any trouble which exists is here in Canada, but that as long as we have to go overseas to seek amendments it means that it is going to be very easy to carry on as we have been carrying on and football important problems backward and forward between the Dominion and the provinces.
In the preparation of this matter I should acknowledge my debt to John S. Ewart, John W. Dafoe, Norman McL. Rogers, F. R. Scott, R. K. Finlayson, A. Grant Dexter, Brooke

British North America Act
Claxton, Eugene Forsey, and others, and to urge that now, with the Canadian League, Canadian clubs and many other similar organizations, and different newspapers taking up and discussing this question, the time is ripe for a full consideration of our constitutional problem by this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words
in regard to the very important matter which has been placed before the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). He has opened the discussion of a very broad and very involved problem, and I congratulate him upon the deep study he has given to the matter and the clear and pointed method in which he has elaborated his case before the house.
I think the house will agree with me, however, that the problem is one which is fraught with many very serious and very grave difficulties. This question of the constitution in Canada is now sixty-three years of age. We have progressed for sixty-three years under our present constitution, and on the whole I think the house will agree that our constitution has worked well. It is true that during the course of those sixty-three years some thirty-one amendments to our constitutional act have been sought from the imperial parliament, and I believe I am correct in saying that upon only one occasion was the advice of the provinces sought in regard to any of the proposed amendments. That occasion was with regard to the question of increased subsidies for the various provinces, but when the provinces were actually consulted on the question their opinions seem to have been disregarded. An amendment was made to our act not in accordance with the views expressed by the provinces at that time.
However, I agree that the time has come when we should seriously consider this whole question of amendments to the Canadian constitution. Last April a Dominion-provincial conference was held in the city of Ottawa, at which all the provinces were represented. The conference was called for the purpose of considering a single proposal set out in the invitation to the various provinces, namely the draft statute of Westminster. The invitation was confined to a discussion of that single question, but notwithstanding the precise language of the invitation, several representatives of the various provinces did have the idea that the general subject of amendments to the Canadian constitution was to be discussed and considered on that occasion. There is no doubt that in many of the provinces there is a fairly active movement for some better understanding as between the
federal and provincial authorities, and I believe the time is near at hand when the wliole question will be fully considered by representatives of this parliament and of the various legislatures, in the hope that some common ground may be found.
I think one cannot criticize the constitution of Canada, as it is often criticized, without having regard to the manner and method in which it was originally adopted. There is a little history in regard to the matter which is always worth remembering. As far back as the year 1864, or perhaps 1865, the question of the confederation of the British provinces in North America became acute, and the best brains of the Canada of those days and of the other provinces which now constitute Canada, as they existed then, were enlisted in solving the problem which then arose. In no British dominion was there in existence at that time a confederation similar to what was subsequently adopted for Canada, but there is no doubt that there was a model which was very largely made use of by the fathers of confederation in this country. That model was to be found in the federal system which then existed on the southern side of the international boundary line. Federal system as it obtained at that time in the United States, however, was said to be the cause of great difficulty; it was said to be the active cause of the civil war, which had been waged in that country between 1861 and 1865. Our forefathers had that example before them and they determined to avoid, as far as possible, the difficulties which beset the United States system. Their idea was to adopt a federal system with a strong federal government, whereas the theory of the United States system was strong state government with less federal authority. The framers of the Canadian constitution reversed the situation as it existed in the United States, and, in the apportionment of powers and jurisdiction as between federal and provincial authority, you will note that separate and distinct powers are granted to the provinces. Under sections 92 and 93 these powers are enumerated and the provinces are plainly told: these are your legislative powers. And in respect of these powers the legislatures of this country are supreme. Their powers are plenary. They are just as supreme within their own legislative jurisdiction as we in this parliament are in regard to our powers. But the remainder of legislative power of every kind was placed under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. It is true that certain specific powers are placed in section 91 as appertaining to the Dominion of Canada. But the general residuum rests with this parlia-

British North America Act
ment. In the United States the system was the reverse: all the residuum there rested with the state authorities.
Now, in considering our constitution it is well to keep that distinction always in mind. The object, the conclusion, the determination of the fathers of confederation was to form n strong cental government and to give certain designated rights to the various provinces of this Dominion. And on that theory the constitution was built up. Whether or not a treaty or an agreement was reached by the representatives of the various sections of Canada which were represented at the preconfederation conference, whether an agreement or treaty was actually reached, I know not. But something in the nature of an agreement was reached, and as a result thereof the British North America Act was drafted.
I am not inclined to view the pre-confederation arrangement as a strict or binding agreement. I am rather inclined to think that the fathers of confederation determined to form a new political entity, that all parties were willing to cast in their lot with that new political entity, in which each province or section of this country should have representation, and to agree that only such powers as were specifically given to the province should remain there. And therefore I have always contended that for the purpose of Dominion legislation all the provinces of Canada are represented in this parliament to-day. That, at all events, is my view of the system under which this country is governed.
When the conclusion was reached and the matter submitted to the imperial parliament, it was submitted as a form of agreement which had been accepted by all parties to constitute a new political entity. And when the act was passed that new political entity had legal force. We were proclaimed a Dominion on the 1st of July 1867, How came the power of amendment to the constitution to be omitted from the British North America Act in respect of federal powers? I submit, Mr. Speaker, it was not by accident that that omission occurred; it was clearly by design: because care was taken in the first subsection of section 92 of the act to provide that each province should have the right to amend ita own constitution as it might see fit. But in regard to the question of amendments with respect to federal rights, the act is absolutely silent. I contend, therefore, that the omission was by design. It was considered that there were certain rights, certain privileges provided for in that act which should be guaranteed to the Dominion of Canada; and the guarantor 
in that respect was the imperial parliament which passed the British North America Act.
The question now is: Has the time come for formulating some plan whereby our act may be amended by this parliament? Certain it is that there are many provisions in the British North America Act which appertain solely and exclusively to this parliament, and I, for one, can see no reason why this parliament should not of its own action make provision for amendments to these various sections as it should see fit. For instance, there are certain sections appertaining to the election of a Speaker of this House of Commons; there are certain sections appertaining to the constitution of a quorum in this house; surely, Mr. Speaker, there is power in this house to make amendments in respect of such matters without consulting the provinces.
My contention has always been that in all matters appertaining to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada the parliament of Canada has the right, and should have the right expressed, to make such amendments to the constitution as it shall see fit. But, on the other hand, the rights of the provinces of the country are just as plenary, just as high as the rights of this parliament. Can this parliament, therefore, by amendment or alteration of any kind, interfere with the rights which are specially set apart as matters of provincial jurisdiction and provincial concern, without the consent of the various provinces of Canada? Many of the questions which have been brought to the attention of the house to-night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are questions upon which the provinces of Canada maintain that they have exclusive jurisdiction. Can we then, without their consent, amend or alter the constitutional act of this country in respect of such questions? I submit that we cannot. In respect of any matters arising under section 92 or section 93 of the British North America Act, this parliament cannot, without the consent of the various provincial legislatures, amend the British North America Act in any respect. And how are we going to obtain that consent-because it is in regard to these very questions that the difficulty from day to day arises as between provincial and Dominion jurisdiction. If this parliament, for instance, were to seek an amendment to our constitutional act in regard to municipal institutions-I am putting some pointed cases

to take from the provinces legislative jurisdiction in respect of such institutions, would anyone say for a moment that we had the right to make such amend-

British North America Act
ment without the positive assent of the provinces? Suppose, again, we were to propose, by an amendment in this parliament, to take the administration of our criminal law from the various provinces of Canada-because the administration of law is specifically given to the provinces by section 92 of the act-do you think that this parliament would be justified in making an amendment of that kind without the consent of the provinces? Or suppose we were to seek to interfere in any way with the question of property and civil rights, which concerns many of the questions which my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre had in his mind: could it be fairly said that there is power in this parliament to change the legislative jurisdiction in respect of property and civil rights without the positive assent of the provinces? And I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, it is in regard to these very matters that we shall never get the consent of the provinces, because the provinces value very highly the jurisdiction to legislate in respect of these matters, which jurisdiction has been conferred upon them by the British North America Act.
I mention these matters merely to point out the serious difficulties, the practical difficulties that are ahead of us when we discuss the question of amendments to the British North America Act.
Let me put another case. We understand what the representation in this house consists of; we know what each province is entitled to have in this House of Commons and also in the upper chamber. We know that anomalies exist in that respect and that one small province would appear to be entirely over-represented, having regard to the representation of some of the larger provinces. But could anyone say for a moment that parliament, of its own free will, would be entitled to change the representation of the various sections of Canada either in this house or in the Senate? I submit we would not. That goes to the very root of the whole question. A question of that kind is fundamental. It was upon those figures that we agreed and for sixty years we have carried on. I submit no power would be given to us to change the representation of the various provinces as they exist in Canada to-day, without the consent of the provinces interested.

Is it not
true that that very thing was done and the entire balance of representation upset at the time British Columbia entered confederation?

speechtext:
That is not my view of
the matter. I know there have been alterations but they have always been tacitly agreed to. I am discussing the question where some province does not agree. What kind of consent must one require to make an amendment such as I have suggested? Is it only of the single province concerned? Is it of a majority of the nine provinces which make up confederation? Or is it the complete, unanimous assent of the whole nine provinces that is required before any alteration can be made? We know the provincial legislatures esteem very highly the legislative rights which they exercise. We know they consider that their powers are just as plenary as are the powers of this parliament, and I am inclined to think they will resent any suggestion on the part of this parliament in any way to limit or diminish their powers. During the recent conference which took place in April I had an informal discussion and I know many of the provinces want to change the sections of the act dealing with the question of taxation. I know some of the provinces want to change those sections of the act dealing with the incorporation of companies, and so on. But they do not desire to give way or limit in any way their own powers. What they desire to do is rather to encroach upon the powers which we claim belong to the federal government.

speechtext:
They had certain rights,
and we likewise had certain rights. There is a cleavage in respect to these matters.
Another serious question that is bound to arise and in regard to which we may in the future have to ask for some change in our constitution, is that of appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. As to that question opinion seems to be divided. Experience in Canada shows that many of the appeals that go to the privy council do not go directly from the Supreme Court of Canada, but rather from the courts of the various provinces. We in this country had a rather rude awakening in 1926 when the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council handed down a judgment in a case that is rather well known in Canada, that of Nadan and the King, which decided that section 1025 of the Criminal Code of Canada was ultra vires. By section 1025 it had been provided in this country that there should be no appeals in certain cases to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, but in the Nadan case, the appeal went directly from the courts of Alberta to the privy council. They did not ask our leave to appeal; they wen*
British North America Act

there as of right. The privy council in its judgment held that they had a right to appeal to that August body for justice, and at the same time held that our section 1025 of the criminal code, which forbade them that right, was beyond the powefs of the parliament of Canada. There possibly will be some conflict in regard to the views of the various provinces in respect to those appeals. Should we ask that this parliament have the right to amend the constitution to provide that there shall be no appeals to the privy council from the Dominion of Canada, or on the other hand should we ask that parliament have an amendment enacted to provide that in all cases there shall be appeals to the privy council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
It may be revived in that way, and I think I am safe in saying that by the first of December next the Colonial Laws Validity Act will probably be repealed so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned. It is under that Colonial Laws Validity Act that the difficulty in regard to these appeals has largely arisen. In all these questions there is in regard to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council a bit of history that it is perhaps worth while remembering. There was a time some seventy or eighty years ago when there was no Colonial Laws Validity Act in existence, but the common law of England was in existence and the common law of England provided that if any colony made a law that was repugnant to the law of England, the law of that colony should be void in so far as it was repugnant to the law of England. In Australia, or in one of the states of Australia, one of the judges gave such a bread interpretation of the common law doctrine, that the people were almost in arms. Practically all the important laws of Australia or of that colony in Australia were being set aside by this judge on the ground that their laws were repugnant to the laws of England. The Colonial Laws Validity Act was passed in the first instance not as a restrictive measure at all, but as an enabling measure. It was passed for the purpose of letting the people in South Australia and, I think, in South Africa know they had rights, and so long as they confined their laws within certain limits, they should not be declared illegal. But subsequently in its actual operation it was found that it hampered many of the dominions, including

the Dominion of Canada, and as a result of the conferences which were held in 1921, 1926, 1927, and the recent one, we have at last reached the point where there will be submitted to this parliament a proposal which, if ratified, will be sent forward to the imperial parliament and in December next a statute known as the statute of Westminster will be passed, which will obviate the difficulty in the future by repealing the Colonial Laws Validity Act so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned.
But this is only one matter in regard to which our difficulties arise. I see practical difficulties-they crop up almost every day in this country7-as between provincial and federal jurisdiction. They are difficulties which are not insurmountable. We have had many of them in the past. We have overcome them in some way. It may be there have been five hundred constitutional cases decided by the courts in the last sixty years, but we have managed to muddle through and we all think our sixty-three years' experience has, on the whole, been a most satisfactory one. But the time is coming, perhaps the time is at hand, when some very critical questions are arising, and perhaps the most critical is in regard to the question of provincial and federal taxation. I agree with the suggestion that in the near future a conference should be summoned for the express purpose of considering some modus operandi upon which we can proceed to secure the right to amend the constitution of the Dominion of Canada. I do not think the language of the motion is sufficient at all. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has included a clause to the effect that he would preserve the rights of minorities by some kind of security or guarantee. Supposing he did; supposing the rights of all minorities were just as fully secured, assured and guaranteed as they are to-day under the British North America Act. That is not the difficulty that I see. He has still to elucidate some plan whereby he can from a basis of agreement in regard to matters which are provincial to-day, and which I think should be federal, and perhaps in regard to some matters which are federal to-day, and which perhaps might be better attended to by the provinces. In this proposal there should be a guarantee of provincial autonomy, because I -for one would not consent to lay hands upon any of those subjects in regard to which the provinces are expressly charged with legislative authority. I would not be one to lay hands upon any provincial rights in respect of those questions which arise under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act without the express consent of the provinces con-

British North America Act
cemed. Those are the difficulties, and only some of the difficulties, which must be overcome, but I think that all these difficulties may in the end be satisfactorily arranged. I am by no means hopeless of the situation. I am entirely hopeful, and I think it would be well for this parliament if not at this session, at some subsequent session, to appoint a committee specially charged with the consideration of this question. We must prepare our case here before we call a conference, and it is a case that will require a great deal of preparation.
I do not accept in full the views of some of the provinces, such as the province of Ontario, as expressed last autumn before the Imperial conference which met at London. With some of those views I am in harmony, but with respect to many of them I think the province is carrying its case rather too far. But we cannot hold a conference without preparation. AVe must know in the first instance what we are prepared to agree on ourselves. Having reached that point I shall heartily favour the summoning of a conference of the provinces with the Dominion authorities to see what plan can be worked out so that in the future this parliament may be able to make the necessary amendments to our constitution.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
This is a very important matter, Mr. Speaker, and it is of special interest at the present time owing to developments that have taken place recently, and in view of the proposed conference to be held at some future date between the provinces and the Dominion to deliberate on this question. It is imperative, therefore, that all the students of our constitutional system, indeed, that all the citizens of Canada, should give consideration to this very important problem, and I am rather grateful to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. AAroodsworth) for bringing forward this resolution were it only that it direct the attention of the people of Canada to the matter.
First I must say that I agree entirely with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that the provinces are also interested in this matter, and that a change in the mode of amending our constitution is a fundamental one as to which the provinces have a right to be consulted, and on which they have a right to express their opinion. The British North America Act-my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has related the historical events that preceded it-was a compromise. It was an arrangement which was effected by Upper and Lower Canada more particularly, but ir. which Ne~ Brunswick and Nova Scotia also joined. It was to put an end to a situation which had brought the country to the verge of civil strife. The provinces
which existed at that time were British colonies, self-governing colonies, and they agreed to relinquish some of their powers and to entrust them to a central authority. They did that subject to certain conditions, some more or less important, others essential; and without those conditions being agreed to confederation could not have taken place. The provinces kept for themselves jurisdiction and power in certain local matters, in civil matters, home rule in matters which more intimately concerned themselves, and they gave to the central government jurisdiction in all matters which affected the people generally in all the provinces.
The British North America Act, as I have already had occasion to note, is not only the charter of the Dominion of Canada; it is also the charter of the provinces. Their powers and their jurisdiction are fixed and determined by that act. The powers and the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada are also fixed and determined by that act It is in many cases a complicated and delicate matter to determine where the jurisdiction of the Dominion ends and where that of the provinces begins. The problem has given rise to many difficulties and to much litigation. I must say to the hon. member for AATnnipeg North Centre in that connection that when the power to amend our constitution is given to Canada, with the consent and the cooperation of the provinces, I believe he is wrong in believing that litigation over the constitution will automatically come to an end. The constitutional act, whether it is the work of the parliament of Canada in conjunction with the provinces, or whether it is an imperial act. will always give rise to difficulties, and the courts will have to pronounce upon them.
Mr. AArOODSWORTH: I think the coming conference ought tc exclude all lawyers.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend need express too much sympathy for the lawyers in connection with the change he is advocating.
Under the conditions as they are to-day, we have the right to amend our constitution. As a matter of fact, it has been amended in many instances. I think my hon. friend said that it had been amended thirty-four times since confederation. But those amendments have to be made through the statute enacted by the imperial parliament. In that matter the imperial parliament is not really a dominating power; it acts as a trustee and as a guarantor, and merely gives effect to the will of the Canadian people. The present system is due to conditions of our social life in Canada as they existed at the time of
British North America Act

confederation. Times have changed, however, and to-day the Dominion of Canada is not the colony it was in 1867. I am in accord with the principle that Canada and the Canadian people should have the right when they see fit to amend their own constitution, and when the provinces, which also are parties to the agreement, agree that a change should be made. At the present time the system of amending the constitution is rather vague, and not altogether consistent in every respect. The only suggestion is, as the Minister of Justice has mentioned: Have the provinces been consulted? The constitution has been changed many times without the consent of the provinces being sought. It was changed in 1907 in the matter of provincial subsidies, and at that time the province of British Columbia did not agree to the change. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that Sir Richard McBride proceeded to London and was heard before a committee of the imperial parliament. There he succeeded in having a certain word, or two words, added to the act, to the effect that the mode of payment that had been agreed upon would not be final, as had been provided in the act passed by this parliament.

I think that the amendments to the constitution could be divided into two classes: first those which would affect the provinces, which would add powers to the federal parliament and in that way affect provincial rights. In such cases surely the British parliament, even under the situation as it exists to-day, would not agree to pass a law to effect the change. Then the other class would be amendments which would give broader effect to the federal power within its own jurisdiction. I agree that the provinces under the constitution as it is need not be consulted, and that was the position taken by various prime ministers on other occasions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have said that the system to amend the constitution is vague. We really do not know what are the amend-

ments in respect to which the assent of the provinces should be first received and those in respect to which such consent is not necessary. However, although the imperial parliament acts only as a trustee, it nevertheless, as I said, constitutes legal subordination on our part to have to ask the imperial parliament to ratify any change we like to make. As my hon. friend from Winnipeg has said, Canada is the only dominion at the present time which has not the right to amend its own constitution. All the other dominions have that right. I will go further and say that Canada is the only country in the world having a federal system of government the constitution of which does not provide for an amendment and for a change by the country of that constitution should occasion arise. The United States have a federal system. There, as hon. members know, the constitution may be changed by a vote of two-thirds of both houses of congress, and such change has to be ratified by three-quarters of the states. Australia also has that right. Germany, which has had a new constitution since 1921, has the same right. The Reichstag can amend its own constitution provided a majority of two-thirds of the members agree to the change. Switzerland also has that right; there again a majority of two-thirds of the members is necessary and the proposed change has to be approved by the people. In Australia the same condition exists. A majority of two-thirds is necessary, and then the action has to be ratified by the states and even by popular vote. A similar or almost similar condition exists in New Zealand. In the Argentine republic a similar condition exists, the constitution may be changed by a majority of two-thirds of the Chamber. Canada, I repeat, is the only country in the world which does not possess that power. I believe an arrangement could be arrived at between the various parties to our constitutional pact by virtue of which we in Canada should have that power, with all the proper safeguards regarding provincial rights and the rights of minorities.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Suppose we have the
right to amend our constitution, does the hon. member think we could amend the constitution of any of the provinces?

speechtext:
No, no. I say that this should be done by cooperation. The provinces at the present time have the right to amend their own constitution, except with regard to the office of the lieutenant-governor; but on the question of the respective jurisdiction of the Dominion and the provinces, there is no doubt that this could not be changed by

British North America Act
either without agreement with the other. That is what I submit, and that is I think the solution of our problem, which is certainly fraught with many difficulties. Because there again how will that consent be obtained, and in what manner shall it express itself? Shall we require the unanimous consent of the provinces to every change that might be sought? I know that this will be the opinion of some, but with that I could not agree. This would make our constitution, I think, too rigid an instrument, and it would be contrary to the principles of the British constitution, which after, all is an instrument of progress. We must have a constitutional instrument which can possibly be altered to suit new facts, new ideas, and so keep progress with the progress of the country.
I was reading some time ago a work published by Dr. William Bennett Munro, a professor at Harvard, and who, I am told, is a Canadian, on The Governments of Europe, and I agree with the views he expresses as regards amending a constitution. He says:
The amending process may fairly be called the most important feature of any constitution. The purpose of a constitution is to preserve order but it cannot preserve order unless it promotes progress->and it cannot promote progress unless it is capable of being amended either formally or by judicial interpretation to meet the new needs that arise. A constitution should not be too easy to amend, for in that case it will fail to secure order, stability, and continuity in the nation's political life. Nor, on the other hand, should it be too difficult to amend, for it will then clog the wheels of political progress and serve as an incentive to coups d'etat or revolutions. The ideal amending process is one that assures stability without impeding the normal development of political and economic activities among the people. On this general principle all makers of constitutions have been substantially agreed, but they have been far from agreement as to the methods whereby the ideal can be attained.
I think those views are correct. A constitution should not be too easy to amend; on the other hand, it should not be too difficult to amend as the necessity arises. Again I say that to insist on having the consent of all the provinces to every change would be asking almost an impossibility; to ask that either British Columbia in the west or Prince Edward Island in the east should be able to block a change with which it is essential for the federal power to go ahead within the limits of its jurisdiction on certain matters, I do not think would be right; but on essential matters, such matters, for instance, as the protection of minorities, of language, of schools, as they are inserted in the British North America Act, I believe it should not be possible to make a change without the consent of all.

I do not want to enter into a discussion of that question, but I think if the hon. gentleman will read Professor Zimmern's book, The Third British Empire, he will find that is exactly the position in which the British Empire found itself in 1926 or about that time. Professor Zimmern is a far greater authority on that subject than I am; all I could do would be, to express my private opinion, in which I am sure the hon. gentleman is not interested.
During the past twelve years in particular this country, in common with the other dominions, has made most extraordinary progress in regard to this very thing which is mentioned by Mr. Brooke Claxton, selfdevelopment, so that to-day we have laid down this principle, that equality of status is, in so far as the United Kingdom and the dominions are concerned, the root principle governing our inter-relation. The old colonial position is past, or is rapidly passing. The Governor General has ceased to be the representative of the government of the United Kingdom; now he is the direct representative of His Majesty to this country. Even the position of the king has changed, for now he is clearly and definitely the king of Canada and appoints his viceroy on advice of Canadian ministers only, and the treaties that we enact by our own right contain words to that affect. "The King, in respect of the Dominion of Canada" is the phraseology actually used. We are, as it is set forth in the report of the recent conference, in no way subordinate in respect of any of our relations, internal or external, to any' other government in the commonwealth of British nations or any other government at all. We appoint our own ambassadors; we make our own treaties; shortly we are to pass the statute

I would ask my hon. friend to let me go on. All that we possess is the power to ask another parliament to do for us what we cannot do ourselves, but I am very glad to-night to hear the unanimous opinion of this house as expressed so far that we should have the power, the right to amend the constitution. I submit that legally the parliament of the United Kingdom can destroy, remove, amend or modify what we call the constitution of Canada without even consulting this country. The British North America Act is not a treaty; it is not a compact, it is not a contract, by the -widest stretch of the imagination. The British North America Act is only a statute of the United Kingdom, nothing more and nothing less. The only body that can effect that statute, naturally, is the body which created
it, and that is the parliament of the United Kingdom. That is the proud position in which we find ourselves.
Hon. members have referred to this act as a contract; they have submitted that it is so much of a contract that the provinces must be consulted before amendments are submitted to the parliament of the United Kingdom. With all due respect I think my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice had some views of his own to express in that regard not long ago. I submit that there is no evidence, at any time, by either enactment or resolution, of any effect whatever upon which this claim can be based or entailing the consulting of the provinces. As a matter of fact the contrary is the case. On almost every occasion on which this parliament and the senate were called upon to consider amending the constitution, or rather a petition for the amendpaent thereof, the opposition raised this question of the right of the provinces to consultation and assent. All the way down the history of constitutional amendments you will find the point, raised that this is a contract and that this parliament has no power to change the contract without consulting the provinces. On every occasion this parliament rejected the opinion so expressed and proceeded to request the amendment without consulting the provinces.
Take next the classic case which has been mentioned in this debate, the case of 1907, with respect to the adjustment of subsidies. Consultation with the provinces had taken place prior to the meeting of parliament, but that consultation was not for the purpose of securing the consent of the provinces to the amendment but merely of getting their agreement to the terms of the change in subsidy. That was all. Moreover, it is to be noted that there is one definite illustration beyond any other-and this confirms me in my belief -to show that hitherto there has been no obligation upon this parliament to secure the consent of the provinces in regard to amendments to the constitution. I refer to the fact that British Columbia and Prince Ediward Island disagreed with the proposed amendment. Both of these provinces passed resolutions through itheir legislative chambers protesting against the terms and one, British Columbia, vigorously resisted them. One of the members representing Prince Edward Island in the house at that time spoke, he said, on behalf of the government and the people of that province, and placed himself in direct opposition to the proposed amendment. But it made no difference; the petition for the amendment was agreed to by this parliament
British North America Act

and went forward. When it went to London, Mr. McBride, the premier of British Columbia, accompanied the delegation and presented himself to protest against the passing of the legislation. It just happened by good fortune that there had been inserted in that bill three words-really two-which were utterly unnecessary and absolutely inapplicable in any statute, especially one such as this. Those words were, "final and unalterable." Those words, I say, were altogether inapplicable, and obviously so; because no amendment to any constitution, not even indeed to a statute of parliament, can be declared by one parliament to be final and unalterable for the simple reason that the succeeding parliament can do what it will with that enactment. And so, to save Mr. McBride's face, Mr. Chamberlain decided to have those words struck out, so that when Mr. McBride came home he was in a position to say that the honour of the province had been vindicated and a constiu-tional crisis obviated.
Bet us go back to 1869, when it was proposed to increase the subsidy to Nova Scotia. The Hon. Mr. Blake rose in the house and protested. He is reported as having said:
It was impossible to suppose that the representatives of the lower provinces had consented to the British North America Act with the understanding and knowledge that it could at any time be changed by a majority in the Canadian parliament.
Very striking words, these. A little later the Hon. Mr. Wood moved an amendment in which he held that the financial arrangements then in the act were a matter of treaty and that even parliament had not the power to change the terms.
Now, if ever there was an illustration of the right claimed by some that the provinces be consulted, it was then furnished. Here was the very essence of the claim of provincial rights-that the consent of the provinces was necessary. The Hon. Mr. Holton spoke. He held that the union was a pact or a treaty between the provinces, and he argued therefrom that they should be consulted. But what happened? The simple result was that the government's proposal was ratified in both houses. As to the contention that consent was necessary by the provinces, it did not succeed but was clearly rejected by parliament.
In connection with the Manitoba Act of 1870, confirmed by the imperial parliament in 1871, it is interesting to note what a well-known constitutional student and authority, John W. Dafoe, said in his article with reference to revising the constitution. That article 
appeared in Queens' Quarterly, the winter issue of 1930, and in it this authority states:
Considerable light is thrown upon the ideas current at that time with respect to the procedure to be followed in securing constitutional legislation by the discussion in the Canadian parliament, which preceded the passage of the British North America Act, confirming the Manitoba Act of 1870 by the imperial parliament in 1871.
The following are the words to which I wish to direct attention particularly:
If it was the understanding at the time of confederation that the provinces were to be parties, at least to the point of giving their consent, to constitutional legislation, it is a little remarkable that no province took exception to the admission to the family of Manitoba under special conditions as to representation, nor to the extensive powers conferred upon the Dominion by the British North America Act of 1871 for the establishment of new provinces.
There, if ever, was an opportunity offered, such as one cannot imagine unless it be the one in 1869; and yet there was no protest, no insistence even in the house, on the part of the advocates of provincial rights, upon the right of the provinces to be consulted.
In 1914 the House of Commons unanimously approved an address to the imperial parliament to change the representation in the Senate. Any student of constitutional history in this country will realize that that did directly affect the original terms of the so-called pact, especially in regard to the province of Quebec. The Senate was regarded as embodying a certain balance for the protection of such rights, and any modification thereof, any adjustment of representation in connection therewith, should certainly have been a matter for consultation with the provinces, if there is validity in the contention that the provinces should be consulted. But what is the fact? This house proceeded unanimously to pass the resolution. The bill went to the Senate and there Senator Dandurand held that approval of the older provinces, or at least consultation with them, should have been effected. But he did not even insist upon their approval; he held that at least there should have been consultation. And observe that in that case it had been the intention of the government to seek to bring about this material change by order in council. It was on that occasion that a motion was introduced-I forget who it was that introduced ,it-determining that in future amendments should be sought on petition of parliament and not of the government. The matter dropped, because the Liberals in the Senate insisted upon attaching to the resolu-

tion a rider to the effect that it should not take effect until the end of that parliament. The leader of the House of Commons at the time refused to accept the Liberal suggestion and the proposed resolution was dropped.
, In 1915 Sir Robert Borden again brought the address to the attention of parliament. There was very little debate in the Commons. ,No question was raised as to the consent of the provinces being required. As soon as the proposal reached the Senate, Senator Bostock, without any reference to the question of the consent of the provinces, once more added the proviso for delay and it was accepted by the leader of the house and by the house. It passed both houses and became, in effect, an application for amendment. And again there was no consultation with the provinces. I may observe, by the way, in connection with the debate that took place in this house following the insistence of the Liberal majority in the Senate at that time upon adding to the resolution their delaying amendment, that some caustic remarks were made; and one .of the most caustic and bitter was a lecture to the Senate, read in th'is house by the then Honourable Richard Bedford Bennett, the same gentleman I believe who is now the leader of the government.
