May I submit, in connection with the question of the complete consent of the provinces, it would be a tremendously serious thing if at any time this country were to acquiesce in the contention that the unanimous approval of the provinces should be secured before any amendment to the constitution is requested? It is exceedingly fortunate that so far this form of procedure has not been established, nor has at any time the requirement of consent of the provinces been established in law or in fact.
In view of the growth and of the importance of the Dominion to-day, in view also of the root principle of equality, in view of the expensive and irritating litigation entailed in an effort to cover matters that were never dreamed of by the fathers of confederation and to stretch the hitherto useful but now
almost outworn constitution to cover those points-in view of all this, it is certainly time to consider calmly and with the most meticulous care what attitude we should take in connection with this proposal. The constitution as we call it, is no sacred tablet. It should not be permitted to shackle our progress or in any way to hamper the evolution, social, economic or political, of this country, and certainly we are entitled now to seek that amendments to the act may be applied by us in our own right and that we shall not be under the obligation of appealing for them to another parliament. That is the smallest step that I would take. Is it not amazing that to-day in spite of all our boasted development of status we do not possess what every Canadian club or board of trade or horse racing organization possesses? These have constitutions of their own and power to amend them. Even our provinces have the right to amend their constitutions.
Speakers who have preceded me have referred to the position in respect to this matter in other of the dominions. In the South African Act of 1909, in the Australian Act of 1900, and in the Irish Free State Act of 1922, provision is made in every case for the amendment of the constitution.

We find that in comparison with these other
British North America Act

countries, we are relatively in a strait-jacket sixty years old. The problem facing us resolves itself into two heads: first the formulation of an amendment. How should this house or this parliament do this? How can Canada best express what she wants? It has become clear to me in recent years in particular, because of the insistence of the provinces on increasing their rights, that we can no longer escape the necessity, no longer escape what I think we are bound to regard as an obligation in the interest of peace, order, and good government, to consult the provinces. I am forced to that conclusion. Picking up again that excellent article by Brooke Claxton, I find he uses this language in regard to it. He deplores the increase of provincial power to the exclusion or diminution of federal power. To some degree I agree with him as did, I think, almost all speakers who preceded me. In this article he calls attention to this. He says:
The weight, of decision has swung backwards and forwards between provincial and federal rights, now favouring the one and now the mher. Since the case of Russell versus the Queen (1882) the general trend has been in favour of provincial rights and array from the express intention of the fathers of confederation to strengthen the central government. It was only in 1922, however, that the general power to legislate for the "peace, order and good government" of Canada became stripped of all effect, except in time of war or general national peril. The federal government, which used to be amply clothed with plenary power, is left without a stitch beyond a sword-belt. The result of all this has been to weaken the federal government's hands and to strengthen the provinces, to weaken national feeling and to strengthen sectional and provincial feeling, to cool the spirit of self-sacrifice and cooperation that during the tvar joined the country from end to end. "Provincial patriotism flourished vigorously under the fostering care of judicial decisions."
I am sure I hear those sentiments echoed in many mouths to-night.
Mr. LaVERGNE : That is. not corroborated by facts or jurisprudence.

speechtext:
Just a minute. He continues:
This is the reverse of the process in the United States, where, since Marshall became chief justice, the general trend has been to strengthen the federal government and the power of the supreme court. Lord Bryce *wrote. "Had the supreme court of the United States of America been in those days possessed of the same spirit of strictness and literalitv which the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has applied to the construction of the British North America Act, 1867, the United States' constitution would never have grown to what it now is.

I submit it now becomes necessary that amendments to the constitution shall receive the support of the voice of all the people in all the legislatures in this country, not unanimously by any means, but by a method to be worked out by such a conference as has been suggested to-night. But the one thing with which I take issue in this amendment, taking it in conjunction with the speech of the mover, is this, that in the discussion of the motion-
That, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that Canada should have the right to amend her own constitution.
-he dwelt almost entirely upon social and economic legislation, all of which may be adjusted by amendment to-day. So that the right of amendment by the Dominion is not involved in the major part of the hon. gentleman's address, and that was really the one thing that bothered me a little bit about it I do not want to strip the provinces of a single vestige of power which they should properly possess, but neither do I want to see the Dominion bereft of its powers and bedevilled by an infernal succession of appeals to litigation on matters so potent to common sense that one cannot for the world understand Why they should ever become matters of litigation. Let me just mention the two latest problems-the problem of aviation and the problem of radio. What interest under heaven can any single province have in the development of either of these great new enterprises which must inevitably be national in character? And yet you have the insistent and growing greed for power of the provinces, ever reaching out to grasp every new development that may take place. That problem has to be met.
The second thing which we have to consider is the enactment of the amendment, and in this connection let me submit to the house that it is not so much an amendment to the constitution that we need, as the creation of our own constitution, %, constitution in which all the necessary constitutional limitations shall be embodied. The occasion of the coming Dominion-provincial conference on this matter might well be the moment for the selection of a royal commission to redraft our constitution or draft a new one, clarrifying it, making clear the relative powers of the Dominion and of the provinces, especially where serious doubts still exist, ironing out many of the difficulties that can be ironed out by the application to the problem of reason and common sense.
* But that would not suffice. After the royal commission had drafted such a constitution,

British North America Act
it should be submitted to the people in a referendum, just as was done in the case of Australia. Let me recall to the members of the house-I think most of them are familiar with it-that the constitution which was drafted by a commission in Australia was submitted to the people of Australia in a referendum, and by a very large majority the first draft was rejected. The commission reconsidered the objections to the first draft, amended the constitution again, and once more submitted it to the people, whereupon it was accepted by a very large majority.
Mr. LaVERGNE: What if the amended constitution were rejected by one province?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: I will deal with that in a moment. In Australia they now have a constitution that comes from the people, and that is what I say Canada should have. The initial draft could be prepared by a commission at the direction of the Dominion-provincial conference. The draft could be submitted by a referendum to the people. If it was not satisfactory to the people, the constitution could be redrafted and submitted again until finally we evolved our own constitution, one arising from and out of the people of this country. After that has been done, I submit that before it should become the formal, official constitution, the draft might secure the consent by resolution of the two major and older provinces, Quebec and Ontario. I make this suggestion in order that we shall ensure definitely that such a constitution would not in any way violate any understood obligations of this country towards the so-called minority. It is a detail which may well await the maturer considerations of the proposed commission.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
You do not believe in
equality of status among the provinces?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
This is not so much a matter of equality of status as a matter of carrying out an obligation-an obligation which we have towards these people, and which I personally, with all others, am willing to accept.
The world has advanced at a great pace since 1867. Science has brought up many new problems, some of which I have mentioned, and which demand solution, problems which certainly were undreamt of by the fathers of confederation and by the parliament of the United Kingdom which enacted the British North America Act. Surely the time has come for this country, which we boast has progressed more than, or at least as much as, any other country on earth, to reconsider in the light of the developments which have 22110-95
taken place in the last sixty years, its whole constitutional fabric and attempt to bring it up to date, instead of doing, as the Minister of Justice said we had done-just muddling through with something that inferentially compels us to muddle through; and he is right. All we are doing to-day is muddling through in a hideous mass of litigation from one year-end to another on questions that could be cleared up measurably by the application of rational, constructive, creative ability. As I said, we .have now to provide for problems that did not exist sixty years ago. Shall we continue to try to stretch this act to cover what it could never have been intended to cover-for that is what we are trying to do to-day-or Shall we now at last prepare our own constitution to meet more fully, more fairly, and more justly the problems of to-day, and make it a constitution more in keeping with the nationhood that we have acquired? Or shall we continue to spend fortunes in futile litigation in an attempt to reconcile the irreconcilable? I stand for a new constitution for Canada-our own.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I intend to take up only a few minutes. I remember the first confederation day in July 1867 as distinctly as if it took place only a year or two years ago. Since that time, at least since I was a boy of fifteen, I have had intimate relations with nearly every prominent man on either side of politics in Canada, and I have heard the constitutional questions as they arose discussed by the men who made the issues. I think that my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Garland) perhaps lacks an intimate knowledge of the atmosphere in which and the conditions under which our constitution has developed. He has referred to a number of instances in which the parliament of Canada decided as to the exact terms of the amendments to be proposed to the imperial parliament, and in respect of which the provinces were not in particular cases consulted. Admitting that the parliament of Canada has control of the treasury of Canada, admitting that the parliament of Canada may distribute, by act of the parliament of Canada, its funds for such purposes as it deems appropriate, then, until last year, I do not remember any amendment to the British North America Act in which the provinces as provinces were intimately concerned. But I do say this, that from the very earliest times the leading public men in both political parties, because there were then only two parties in the main, have proceeded on the basis that in respect of those matters in which the provinces as provinces



British North America Act

were concerned they should be consulted before radical amendments were made to the British North America Act. When I say radical amendments I mean amendments such as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has described-reapportioning the division of legislative jurisdiction between the legislatures of the provinces and the federal parliament.
I quite agree that the time is coming when Canada, by the concerted action of the federal as well as the provincial authorities, may well exercise, the right and legislative power of amending the constitution of Canada. However, in providing ways and means for such amendment we must necessarily make such discrimination as the Minister of Justice made to-night and in which I understood the hon. member for Quebec East, the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), to concur. The constitution of Canada as expressed in the British North America Act, as pointed out by hon. members who have preceded me, deals with certain matters which should be within the competence of this parliament alone to decide. With respect to those matters the provinces are not interested and should not be consulted.
I will go so far as to say that even in certain minor matters a new apportionment of legislative jurisdiction might be made by the consent of the majority of the provinces. But amendments to the main structure of confederation, which forms the basis of the union of our people of different religions and different races, cannot be placed within the jurisdiction of this federal parliament alone if the peace and good order, happiness and contentment of our people is to continue in the future as it has in the past. Before the recent Dominion-provincial conference, simply trying my hand for the amusement of myself and the information of some of my friends, I drafted a clause which might be inserted in the new statute of Westminster with regard to future amendments to the British North America Act. But being present I felt the atmosphere of the recent provincial conference, and it was then quite clear to me that my personal ideas were altogether too radical to secure the approval of the conference. It seemed to me however-and this is merely a personal suggestion-that we might come to an understanding with the provinces to the effect that mere amendments to our own constitution such as parliamentary procedure, the constitution of our own parliament in so far as it does not affect the rights of provinces and their proportional representation therein, should be within the competence of this parliament, exclusively. With
fMr. Cahan.]
regard to those other matters which concern the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces, in contradistinction to the legislative jurisdiction of the Dominion, I think we might possibly find some line of division in respect to which a majority of the provinces concurring might authorize the Dominion parliament to proceed with amendments.
I heard the expression informally upon at least half a dozen occasions from half a dozen representatives of provinces of Canada during the recent provincial conference that it should not be within the competence of one provincial legislature, through indirect action for local and selfish motives, to prevent reforms being carried out which were approved by all the other provinces. I would not speak in terms of disrespect concerning the province of ' Prince Edward Island; I love that island, because it is the neighbour of my native province of Nova Scotia. I hold that province in great respect, and yet I heard it suggested on several occasions that the province of Prince Edward Island alone or the province of Nova Scotia alone should not be placed in the position of being permitted to thwart every measure of public reform desired by the other provinces of the Dominion. That issue must be met. With regard to these other matters, however, which deal with education and the like, which deal with race and language and frame the issues upon which the compromise was reached by the fathers of confederation, those matters certainly should not be changed except with the consent of those provinces which, by reason of their populations being largely of one race or the other, are therefore intimately concerned therein. My proposition was of no great value, but I suggested that the British North America Act might be amended by an act of the parliament of Canada which should pass both houses of parliament either by a clear majority of all the members or by a three-quarters majority in each house.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Or a two-thirds majority.

speechtext:
I am giving perhaps a more conservative safeguard. Before such a measure should receive the assent of the governor general in the name of the king it should within eighteen months thereafter receive the approval of either the governments of the several provinces or the legislatures of the several provinces. I myself favoured the approval of the separate and distinct legislatures. There was a further provision that changes which affected interests of race, religion and education should be concurred in by all the legislatures of all the provinces. It

British North America Act
is along that line that I think the minds of men are working.
I do not believe in putting the whole Canadian constitution into the waste heap. I lived my youth with those men who framed our confederation. Perhaps it was because of my youth and their political stature that I have now so high an appreciation of their great intelligence and ability. I do not think that in this present day, even in this parliament, that we have the same political intelligence- well, perhaps I should not say that. However, there is such a thing as political intelligence. My hon. friend who preceded me spoke of other kinds of intelligence, but in regard to political intelligence I do not think we are in any way superior to the men who sat in the first parliament of Canada. I do not think we are more sincere or more patriotic, and I doubt if we understand the problems of our day more clearly than they understood the problems of their day. It is all nonsense to suggest, as my hon. friend has, that a few businessmen can express a political constitution in such terms of clarity as to preclude litigation with respect to it in the future.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Not at all; I did not say that.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: I understood that to be the suggestion of my hon. friend.

speechtext:
No, I
never referred to businessmen. I referred to a royal commission appointed by an interprovincial conference. I am sure my hon. friend would not take issue with a royal commission.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: I am not taking issue with a royal commission at all.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: It is not fair to say that I spoke of a few businessmen framing a constitution.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman seemed to cast some reflection on the present constitution by reason of the fact that it had given rise to litigation, and to suggest that such litigation was to be obviated' by the new constitution which is to be developed by some means such as he suggested. So long as mortal man finds it difficult to express his thoughts in concise, precise language, so long will thfere be litigation. I do not think that this Canada to-day has men in its midst who are more capable of expressing their views in concise, precise terms that will avoid litigation in the future than were those men who framed our original constitution. It is a matter of sincere congratulation to this country that we have developed as we have with
that consistent cordial cooperation which has distinguished men on both sides and of all parties who have represented Canada in this House of Commons. I sat in this press gallery in 1887 and 1888 as a reporter, with Sir John Macdonald leading the house, with Blake and Cartwright and Mills on the other side, and when Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Mr. Wilfrid Laurier, had hardly emerged into the political prominence to which he afterwards attained. The members of this house are not more intelligent than those men, though as intelligent no doubt in dealing with the problems which we have to deal with as were our predecessors in dealing with the problems of their day. And we will go on and deal with them. We want no revolutionary changes. Let us develop in the future as we have developed for the past sixty years, during which period we have avoided those grave perils and difficulties which had been foreseen from time to time by those who preceded us. To do that we must proceed by cordial cooperation and by consent. I would give to the provinces by consent the largest liberty that it is possible to give them; but I agree with those hon. gentleman who say it is their duty as members of this federal parliament to preserve intact to the fullest extent possible the legislative jurisdiction which we now enjoy, because the exercise of that jurisdiction by a parliament representative of all the provinces, of all the electoral districts of Canada, is absolutely necessary if we are to develop in the future as in the past as a nation under the British crown.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny): Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to think we are wandering far from the resolution. If I understand it well, the resolution is to this effect: whether Canada is to be mistress of her own destiny, to be able to amend her constitution, or whether she is still to be under the imperial act which can be changed only at the will of Great Britain. I 'think that every Canadian proud of being a Canadian will agree with the resolution that Canada should be mistress of her own destiny, of her own constitution.
The resolution provides for the safeguard of the rights of minorities. I dhall come back to that later on. But objections have been raised to the consent of the provinces being necessary to a change in our constitution. In my opinion the provinces, as sovereign colonies, have retained to themselves certain of their original rights, and have delegated the balance to the central power. Whether we like it or not, I cannot see why this parliament should be able to amend the constitution so far as it affects such rights of the provinces
British North America Act

as were guaranteed by article 92 of the British North America Act. That is, their rights cannot be touched by this parliament, and the act in these respects can be amended only by their consent. Every right reserved to the provinces by section 92 belongs to the provinces, and this parliament could not, even by unanimous vote, take those rights away from them. I have heard to-night that this has been done in the past. But I would point out that the resolutions that have been passed from time to time to amend the constitution have not touched the rights of the provinces, except so far as they may have been included in section 91 of the act, in which cases the consent of the provinces was given by the vote in this house of the members representing those provinces.
Now, the question is this: Should Canada be mistress of her own destiny? I think we all agree on that, and if we do not, I am sure the dissenting minority would be very small. But at the same time we must understand that the pact of 1867 was the delegation by sovereign colonies to the central parliament of certain of their rights, reserving others, and the rights so reserved this parliament cannot touch. For instance, we cannot amend the civil code of the province of Quebec; we cannot amend the rights of the provinces with respect to their municipal law. Those rights belong to the provinces, and if we passed any resolution or any statute to curtail or take away those rights we would be disrupting confederation. Of course, there has been litigation. Wherever there is law there must be litigation, and since the code of Justinian, or even before that, since the law of the twelve tables, there has been litigation, and as long as laws are passed, even by the parliament of Canada-although the House of Commons as it is constituted to-day represents the best brains of the country-I am sure there is bound to be litigation regarding their interpretation. But I know this-and here I take issue with my friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland)-that far from the provinces en-croacbing on the central power, experience, jurisprudence and facts have demonstrated that every time that a province and the central power have passed concurrent legislation, the federal legislation was certain to supersede and to nullify the provincial legislation. Therefore, far from encroaching on the central power. I think all the provinces have seen their powers curtailed through the very letter of section 92.
My hon. friend very lightly, and I was going to say very broadly but that is not the word I want, stated that the rights of the

minorities should be preserved. Well, we had the British North America Act, by which the rights of the minorities were to be preserved. More than that, we had the declaration by Lord Carnarvon u'hen moving the adoption of the British North America Act in the House of Lords in 1865 or 1866. He stated that not only the minorities in esse but the minorities in posse should have the same rights the moment they entered union, and that Lower Canada was as just proud of her institutions as was Upper Canada. Lord Carnarvon said that any minority, be it French or English. Catholic or Protestant, the moment it entered the union with a system of separate schools or with certain rights of language, would have those rights preserved.
I ask this House of Commons how this pact has been kept. We have had the British North America Act amended without the consent of this House of Commons. It has been amended in Manitoba, where the rights of the minority have been curtailed by the legislature. I must say that this parliament tried to pass a remedial bill. I do not warn to open old sores, but the remedial bill was not passed, and every hon. member remembers why. Let me quote one point. In 1897, when Sir Charles Tupper was leader of the opposition, he offered the then Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the full support of the opposition if another remedial bill should be introduced. The Conservative government had just fallen over the cause of the minority in Manitoba, and I think there is no page in Canadian history of which a nation should be more proud and of which the Conservative party should be more proud than that which has to do with this action of the old leader of the Conservative party, who had been defeated in 1896 because he stood for the rights of minorities and for justice and liberty in this country.
This will show that in spite of our blunders we still manage to get through. I have heard from some people who call themselves very strong provincial rights-and not to bring any names before this house I shall not name the premiers of Quebec-that Canada should not be mistress of her owrn destiny, that our safeguard was in Westminster and the throne. I believe I am one of the last monarchists in the world just now-certainly I am not of the most convinced monarchists-and no one more than myself believes in the right of petition to the throne. However, I must.go further. I do not agree with the premier of Quebec: I think these are Canadian matters which should be settled between Canadians. I have enough confidence in my English-speaking compatriots to trust the destinies of the minority of this province in their hands.

British North America Act
Probably, and I think undoubtedly, there will be some who will not immediately accept the rights of the minority in this province. There are those who, rightly or wrongly-wrongly, in my opinion-think it is too bad that we should have two languages and two religions in this country. With regard to the two religions, even if the Roman Catholic religion disappeared I think my hon. friends who are not of my faith might find a little difficulty in agreeing among themselves. But let me go further: I know there is a school of thought who say, as they said sixty years ago, that this country must be English, even at the expense of ceasing to be British. I claim the greatest asset of this country is our dual language and our dual civilization, and I have enough confidence in the spirit of fair play and the Canadian spirit of my English-speaking compatriots to trust in their hands, rather than in the hands of Westminster or even the privy council, the destinies of the minorities of this country. That is why I heartily support the motion.
I think these are questions which should be discussed among ourselves. We may have bitter discussions at times, until we come to the conclusion that whether we be of French or English origin, of Catholic or Protestant faith, we have one common ground, and that is our common mother Canada, the land of our forefathers, the only land we care for and the only land to which we owe a duty. For these reasons I humbly support the resolution of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Winnipeg North Centre will close the debate if he speaks now. Does any other hon. member wish to speak?

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
It seems to me,
Mr. Speaker, with the tone of the debate which has taken place this evening, that there would be no great purpose served by putting this motion to a vote. There have been some rather minor objections to the motion; some criticism has been made as to the wording, and some hon. members might not care to support the motion just as it stands. So I feel that as on the whole the motion has received such very general support from all sections of the house, there would be no particular object gained in calling for a vote.
It appears to me that we have indeed made a very great deal of progress in the last few years. I cannot but recall with some amusement that when I first introduced this question seven years ago one of the newspapers printed a fine cartoon in which the Canadian
constitution was represented as a magnificent pillar, while the mover of the resolution was pictured as a tiny mosquito attempting to undermine or break down that pillar. We have, gone beyond that stage, and it is a great gain when we can seriously and dispassionately discuss, a matter of this kind. :
I welcome the suggestion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that next year, or in! the near future, a special committee of this house will be appointed to prepare our case^ In that way we can see what amendments may be necessary, so that when a constitutional conference is called we shall be in a position to handle the matter with some intelligence. That statement from the minister is, I think, all that could be expected as a result of our discussion this evening. I quite agree with the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) in his eulogy of the giants of the older days, with their wonderful political intelligence, and of course all of us who live in these degenerate days must look back with a great deal' of reverence to the men of sixty years ago. At the same time, I would submit that we must work out our own problems in our own day and in our own way. And that is not to show any disrespect to those who have gone before us. As I said in my speech tonight, the men in that day differed from the others in that they were willing to take a chance in having some change from the conditions that had prevailed prior to their time; and we are most truly following in their footsteps when we undertake to make necessary changes in our day. So that, inasmuch as we are now confronted with a new set of circumstances, the only thing for us to do is to endeavour to bring about suitable modifications.
I would take exception again to the statement reiterated by the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) that there was an agreement. I do not wish to attempt to cover the ground which I went over before, but it does seem to me that it is impossible for us, in view of the historical data we have available, to hold that there was any definite agreement as to the terms of the British North America Act. The hon. member is on much safer ground in the sentiments he expressed in the latter part of his short speech. We have come to the point where we can trust one another, and I think the hon. gentleman will recognize that a statement of that kind from him will cause the rest of us to feel not that we must take advantage of any opportunity to get even with him or to get the better of him, but would rather provoke in us a desire to be worthy of such trust.
British North America Act

Mr. LaVERGNE : I think the agreement was arrived at in this way. Sir Alexander Galt, in the name of the minority of Quebec, requested that certain rights should be granted to minorities, either Catholic or Protestant, in all the provinces. It was he who, in the name of the Protestant minority of Quebec, requested that agreement on resolutions from Quebec.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE CANADA TO AMEND HER OWN CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I quite recognize
that certain agreements were made; we had a number of agreements. There were the original agreements of Quebec and London, and finally the British North America Act. Undoubtedly there were certain understandings. But my point is that we cannot hold to those in any hard and fast legal way. The British North America Act is not a contract in the sense of a legal contract. If I may use again the figure I ventured to use before, I would suggest that it is something in the nature of the marriage relationship. We have lived together, and the relationship has changed from a mere contract, so that we now entertain towards one another a certain degree of confidence and good fellowship, and affection if you like. The Dominion of Canada is more than a string of provinces: it is a family. In that sense we get away from the old difficulties as to whether Quebec and Ontario should be consulted, and they alone, since they were the old and original provinces, while the newer provinces are left out. Speaking personally, I may say that as a child I moved from the old province of Ontario to Manitoba. But I am just as much a Canadian as my cousins who remained in Ontario; and if there is to be any consultation I think I am just as much entitled to be consulted as those of my relatives who remained in this province. But that would not be the case if you held us to the old legal idea of Ontario as a distinct entity. Our grandfathers lived in different parts of the country and we may live also in different provinces, but we all live in Canada. The time has come when we should get away from the custom of thinking in purely legal terms. Let us think rather in terms of the actual conditions that prevail, and with a view to working out for the future a constitution which will really meet our needs as we see them to-day.
As my good friend the Secretary of State .(Mr. Cahan), whom I respect highly, was speaking, I could not but recall a resolution which I wrote out in a rather frivolous mood :about a year ago, when the ex-Prime Minister {Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking so much about the British North America Act-we could not get anything done because of it, and so forth. And there was also a good 
deal of talk about the Kellogg pact and the idea of hanging it up in the schools. I know that irony is dangerous, but this is the resolution that occurred to me then as one which possibly might be suitable to place on the order paper:
. Whereas the tide of new and disturbing ideas is removing ancient landmarks, encroaching on hoary tradition, subverting archaic institutions, embarrassing routine administration and threatening established political equilibrium:
Therefore resolved that in the opinion of this house the government, after having obtained the consent of each and all of the provinces, should consider the advisability of hanging a suitably-framed copy of the British Aorth America Act in every schoolroom in Canada.
Cannot we get away from that old idea that we must always have respect for the letter of the pjst? Rather, we should seek to enter into the spirit of the fathers of confederation and to carry out their work along the new lines. I wish to express my own personal gratitude to the members of the house for the very thoughtful and considerate way in which they have received my resolution to-night, and with the consent of the house I beg leave to withdraw it.
Motion withdrawn.
